meta.blurb: In 1513 a Florentine official lost his job when the Medici family came back, and wrote a handbook for rulers on his farm. Machiavelli's advice on winning and keeping power still shocks readers. Is it honest, or a warning?
meta.bible: Niccolò Machiavelli: Florentine official and writer, 1469 to 1527; lost his post when the Medici returned to Florence in 1512; wrote The Prince in 1513 on his farm near Florence; it was printed in 1532, after his death. The Prince: a short book of 26 chapters on how princes gain, keep and lose states. Florence: the Italian city-republic where Machiavelli worked. Medici: the ruling family of Florence. Lorenzo de' Medici: the young ruler to whom the book is dedicated. Italy: at that time a patchwork of small states, often invaded by France and Spain. France, Spain, Rome, Carthage. Cesare Borgia: a ruthless young leader whom Machiavelli studied closely; son of Pope Alexander VI. Pope Alexander VI, Pope Julius II. Romagna: the region Borgia conquered. Remirro de Orco: the harsh governor Borgia sent to Romagna. Moses, Cyrus, Romulus, Theseus: great founders of ancient states. Savonarola: a Florentine preacher who fell when his followers lost faith. Alexander the Great: the Macedonian conqueror; Darius: the Persian king he defeated. Louis XII: King of France who lost his hold on Italy. Agathocles: a potter's son who became ruler of Syracuse by force. Hannibal: the Carthaginian general who kept a mixed army united. Marcus Aurelius: a respected Roman emperor; Commodus: his son, killed by his own court. Caterina Sforza: Countess of Forlì, whose fortress could not save her. Ferdinand of Aragon: King of Spain, admired for bold undertakings. David and Saul: the biblical story of the borrowed armour. Achilles, Caesar, Scipio. Petrarch: the poet quoted in the last chapter. Francesco Vettori: Machiavelli's friend, to whom he wrote. Key terms: Prince, Principality, Republic, Mercenaries, Fortune, Virtù, Fortress, Ministers, Flatterers. Voice and tone: clear, cool and direct; Machiavelli's views are always attributed to him and never presented as the book's endorsement; violence is stated plainly without gore; where scholars disagree, the text says so. Full-length additions. Machiavelli's life: born 3 May 1469; joined the government of Florence in 1498 aged 29; many missions to Louis XII of France, Pope Julius II and the Emperor Maximilian; watched Cesare Borgia in 1502 and 1503; raised a citizen Militia in 1506; Piero Soderini: head of the Florentine republic until 1512; Prato: the town a Spanish army stormed in August 1512; dismissed in November 1512; arrested in February 1513 over a plot of Pietro Paolo Boscoli and freed in March when Giovanni de' Medici became Pope Leo X; retired to his farm at Sant'Andrea near San Casciano; wrote to Francesco Vettori in December 1513. Lorenzo de' Medici is the grandson of Lorenzo the Magnificent. Hereditary states: Ferrara held by its old ducal house. Mixed states: Louis XII and Milan, Ludovico Sforza; Burgundy, Brittany, Gascony, Normandy; the Turk in Greece; Rome, Carthage, Capua, Numantia, Athens, Thebes, Sparta, Corinth; Cardinal Rouen (Georges d'Amboise); Pisa. Chapter 4: Darius; the Turk and the Sultan; Kings of France and their barons. Chapter 6: Moses, Cyrus, Romulus, Theseus, Savonarola, Hiero of Syracuse. Chapter 7: Duke Valentino is Cesare Borgia; Remirro de Orco; Cesena; Senigallia; Vitellozzo Vitelli; Oliverotto; the Orsini and Colonna; Urbino; Pope Pius III. Chapter 8: Agathocles of Syracuse; Oliverotto da Fermo; Giovanni Fogliani, his uncle; Fermo. Chapter 9: Nabis of Sparta; the Gracchi; Giorgio Scali. Chapter 10: the free cities of Germany. Chapter 11: Pope Sixtus IV; Charles VIII of France, who invaded Italy in 1494; Venice; Naples; Pope Leo X. Chapter 12: Francesco Sforza; Filippo Maria Visconti; Carmagnola; Vailà in 1509; Sir John Hawkwood (Giovanni Acuto); Paolo Vitelli; Braccio; Epaminondas; Philip of Macedon; the Swiss. Chapter 13: the Emperor of Constantinople; Charles VII and Louis XI of France; Tacitus. Chapter 14: Philopoemen; Xenophon. Chapter 17: Pistoia; Virgil's Dido; Scipio; Fabius Maximus; the Locrians. Chapter 18: Chiron the centaur. Chapter 19: Annibale Bentivoglio of Bologna; the Canneschi; the Parlement of France; the Roman emperors Marcus Aurelius, Commodus, Pertinax, Julian, Septimius Severus, Albinus, Pescennius Niger, Caracalla, Macrinus, Heliogabalus, Alexander Severus, Maximinus; Aquileia. Chapter 20: Guelf and Ghibelline parties; Pandolfo Petrucci of Siena; Niccolò Vitelli of Città di Castello; Guido Ubaldo of Urbino. Chapter 21: Granada; Bernabò Visconti of Milan; Antiochus, the Aetolians and the Achaeans. Chapter 22: Antonio da Venafro. Chapter 23: the Emperor Maximilian. Chapter 24: Titus Quintius. Chapter 25: Bologna and Giovanni Bentivoglio. Chapter 26: Livy; the battles of Taro, Alexandria, Capua, Genoa, Vailà, Bologna and Mestri; Ravenna in 1512. Afterwards: Discourses on Livy; Mandragola, a comedy; The Art of War, printed in 1521; Florentine Histories, for Cardinal Giulio de' Medici, later Pope Clement VII; the Sack of Rome in 1527; Machiavelli died on 21 June 1527, aged 58, and lies in Santa Croce; The Prince was printed in Rome and Florence in 1532; banned by the Church in 1559; Cardinal Reginald Pole; Christopher Marlowe; Frederick of Prussia wrote Anti-Machiavel in 1740; Rousseau; Machiavellian. Tuscany: the region around Florence, Pisa, Lucca and Siena. Fortuna: luck and circumstance; Virtù: skill, energy and courage. Silesia: a province of Austria, invaded by Frederick of Prussia in 1740; Voltaire edited his Anti-Machiavel; Elizabeth: queen of England, whose stage knew the Machiavel; Henry VI; Richard of Gloucester; The Jew of Malta; Index of forbidden books; Reginald Pole; Clement VII; Blado; Giunta; Risorgimento; Italy became one kingdom in 1861; Imperial troops sacked Rome in May 1527.
chapters: A Clerk, a Rope, a Farm
A Gift for the Young Medici
Why Conquerors Lose What They Win
The Risk of Being Too Good

beats.scene: A young clerk in a plain coat climbs the steps of a Florentine palace
beats.summary: In 1498, aged twenty-nine, Machiavelli becomes a senior secretary of the republic of Florence.

beats.scene: Machiavelli rides a horse along a muddy road towards a foreign court
beats.summary: As a diplomat he travels to France, Rome and the emperor's court.

beats.scene: A grim young duke in black receives Machiavelli in a candlelit castle hall
beats.summary: In 1502 and 1503 Machiavelli studies Cesare Borgia at close quarters.

beats.scene: Farmers in plain jackets drill with long spears in a Florentine field
beats.summary: Machiavelli builds a citizen militia for Florence, because he distrusts hired soldiers.

beats.scene: Spanish soldiers pour through a broken wall into a small Tuscan town
beats.summary: In August 1512 Spanish troops storm Prato, the militia runs, and the republic soon falls.

beats.scene: Machiavelli walks away from the government palace carrying a box of papers
beats.summary: In November 1512 the Medici dismiss Machiavelli and bar him from the palace.

beats.scene: A prisoner hangs by his wrists from a rope in a dim cell
beats.summary: In 1513 he is arrested over a plot, questioned under torture, and then freed.

beats.scene: A small farmhouse among olive trees and woods outside Florence
beats.summary: He retires to his farm at Sant'Andrea, some miles south of Florence.

beats.scene: Machiavelli plays cards with a butcher, a miller and two workers at an inn
beats.summary: By day he cuts wood, then plays cards at the inn with local men.

beats.scene: Machiavelli in fine robes sits at a desk by candlelight with old books
beats.summary: In the evenings he puts on court clothes to read the ancients, and writes a short book on princes.

beats.scene: Machiavelli bows and hands a rolled manuscript to a young nobleman in a hall
beats.summary: Dedication: Machiavelli offers the book to Lorenzo de' Medici, hoping for a place in the new government.

beats.scene: Machiavelli lays old scrolls and papers on a table as a gift
beats.summary: Dedication: the only gift he has is his knowledge of the deeds of great men.

beats.scene: A painter sketches mountains from the valley floor while another sits on a peak
beats.summary: Dedication: like a landscape painter, a man of low rank can still understand princes.

beats.scene: A young lord looks down from a balcony at a man in the square
beats.summary: Dedication: he asks Lorenzo to look down from his high place and see his undeserved bad luck.

beats.scene: A map of Italy marked with large and small states
beats.summary: Chapter 1: every state is a republic or a principality, and this book is about principalities.

beats.scene: A prince with a sceptre stands beside a conqueror holding a sword
beats.summary: Chapter 1: principalities are old or new, won by one's own arms or another's, by luck or skill.

beats.scene: An old king teaches his young son beside a wall of family portraits
beats.summary: Chapter 2: hereditary states are the easiest to keep, because people are used to the family.

beats.scene: Soldiers on the walls of a small castle hold off a besieging army
beats.summary: Chapter 2: the Duke of Ferrara withstood the Venetians and Pope Julius II because his family was old there.

beats.scene: A ruler greets townspeople in a market who wave and smile
beats.summary: Chapter 2: a born prince has less reason to offend, so his people naturally like him.

beats.scene: A stone wall with gaps where the next stones could be fitted
beats.summary: Chapter 2: long rule wipes out the memory of change, because one change always leaves a toothing for another.

beats.scene: Townspeople cheer a conqueror's arrival while an old ruler's banner is torn down
beats.summary: Chapter 3: people change rulers gladly, hoping for better, and are then disappointed.

beats.scene: A new ruler in armour faces angry farmers and hungry soldiers
beats.summary: Chapter 3: the conqueror must injure those he rules, and cannot satisfy those who helped him.

beats.scene: A king's army retakes a rebel city while captured leaders are led away
beats.summary: Chapter 3: a province conquered a second time is lost less easily, as Louis XII found at Milan.

beats.scene: Two neighbouring villages in the same dress join under one banner
beats.summary: Chapter 3: lands with the same language and customs are easy to hold, as France holds Burgundy and Brittany.

beats.scene: A prince in travelling clothes walks through a foreign village among puzzled people
beats.summary: Chapter 3: where language and customs differ, the best remedy is for the conqueror to live there, as the Turk did in Greece.

beats.scene: Settlers build houses on a hilltop while soldiers stand guard in a distant town
beats.summary: Chapter 3: colonies of settlers cost little and hurt few; an army of occupation costs much and angers all.

beats.scene: A prince stands between a weak small state and a large threatening one
beats.summary: Chapter 3: the prince should protect weaker neighbours, weaken the strong, and keep strong foreigners out.

beats.scene: Roman officers stand on a hill in Greece, looking down at an army camp
beats.summary: Chapter 3: the Romans saw trouble from afar and fought wars in Greece rather than wait for them in Italy.

beats.scene: A doctor leans over a pale patient while a worried family waits
beats.summary: Chapter 3: like a wasting fever, trouble in a state is easy to cure early and impossible to cure late.

beats.scene: A French king and a cardinal argue over a map of Italy
beats.summary: Chapter 3: Louis XII made five mistakes in Italy; Machiavelli tells a cardinal that the French do not understand government.

beats.scene: Alexander the Great in armour gazes over a vast Persian plain
beats.summary: Chapter 4: why did the empire of Darius not rebel against Alexander's heirs after his early death?

beats.scene: A sultan sits among his servants, while a French king stands among his barons
beats.summary: Chapter 4: states are governed either by a prince with servants, like Turkey, or by a prince with barons, like France.

beats.scene: A palace under siege, with no one inside willing to open the gates
beats.summary: Chapter 4: the Turk's state is hard to conquer, because his servants cannot be bribed, but easy to hold once he is beaten.

beats.scene: French barons in castles wave to a foreign invader at a gate
beats.summary: Chapter 4: a kingdom like France is easy to enter, because some barons are discontented, but hard to keep.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers fight in a mountain pass among rebellious tribes
beats.summary: Chapter 4: Alexander's empire was like Turkey's and held; the Romans lost Spain, Gaul and Greece to many revolts until memory of the old rulers faded.

beats.scene: A free city's walls and old banner, with a conqueror's army outside
beats.summary: Chapter 5: there are three ways to hold a city used to its own laws: destroy it, live there, or let it keep its laws and pay tribute.

beats.scene: Spartan soldiers install a small council to rule a proud city
beats.summary: Chapter 5: the Spartans held Athens and Thebes through governments of a few friends, but lost both.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers pull down the walls of a burning city
beats.summary: Chapter 5: the Romans destroyed Capua, Carthage and Numantia and kept them; in Greece they tried leaving cities free and had to destroy many.

beats.scene: Citizens of a free city raise their old flag as soldiers retreat
beats.summary: Chapter 5: a city used to freedom never forgets it; Pisa, held by Florence for nearly a hundred years, rose up at once.

beats.scene: Elders argue in a town hall beside an empty throne
beats.summary: Chapter 5: cities used to a prince accept a conqueror easily; republics hate more and are more dangerous.

beats.scene: An archer on a hill aims high at a distant target
beats.summary: Chapter 6: a prince should imitate great men, and aim high like an archer who allows for a far target.

beats.scene: Moses leads a crowd of tired people away from a brick yard
beats.summary: Chapter 6: Moses and Cyrus owed fortune only the opportunity: Israel was enslaved in Egypt, and Persia was unhappy under the Medes.

beats.scene: Romulus marks the line of a new city wall as villagers gather around
beats.summary: Chapter 6: Romulus had to be cast out of Alba, and Theseus found the Athenians scattered; opportunity and ability together made them great.

beats.scene: A lone reformer shows new laws to a doubtful crowd while officials frown
beats.summary: Chapter 6: nothing is harder than introducing a new order, because its enemies are many and its defenders lukewarm.

beats.scene: A reformer stands alone before a crowd while another waits for help from patrons
beats.summary: Chapter 6: a reformer must stand on his own strength; those who must beg for help fail, and those who can use force rarely do.

beats.scene: Armed lawgivers stand before crowds who have fallen quietly into line
beats.summary: Chapter 6: all armed prophets won and all unarmed ones failed, because people change their minds and must sometimes be forced to believe.

beats.scene: A preacher in a Florentine square watches his crowd drift away
beats.summary: Chapter 6: Savonarola of Florence fell when the people stopped believing him, because he had no means to hold them.

beats.scene: A Syracusan captain stands before cheering soldiers in a Sicilian city
beats.summary: Chapter 6: Hiero of Syracuse rose from private life to rule, with only the opportunity from fortune.

beats.scene: A young man in fine clothes receives a crown at the top of stairs
beats.summary: Chapter 7: those who rise by luck or the arms of others rise easily but struggle to stay, like the governors Darius made.

beats.scene: A rough soldier in plain armour stands beside a young duke in black
beats.summary: Chapter 7: two modern examples: Francesco Sforza rose by ability, while Cesare Borgia gained by fortune and lost it.

beats.scene: Pope Alexander VI in rich robes studies a map with his son beside him
beats.summary: Chapter 7: Alexander VI wants to make his son Cesare a prince, but every road is blocked.

beats.scene: King Louis XII signs a paper while a cardinal in red looks on
beats.summary: Chapter 7: the pope helps Louis XII end his marriage, and the French help Cesare in the Romagna.

beats.scene: A young commander in dark clothes leads troops past a captured town
beats.summary: Chapter 7: Borgia conquers the Romagna, but doubts the loyalty of his Orsini soldiers and fears France.

beats.scene: Armed men in a small seaside palace seize their guests at a banquet
beats.summary: Chapter 7: at Senigallia in 1502 Borgia traps the rebel captains; two are put to death that night.

beats.scene: A stern governor in a long coat judges townspeople in a Romagna square
beats.summary: Chapter 7: the Romagna is full of thieves and quarrels, so Borgia sends the harsh Remirro de Orco with full power.

beats.scene: A crowd gathers at dawn in the square of Cesena around a wooden block
beats.summary: Chapter 7: to wash away the people's hatred, Borgia has Remirro put to death in public, and the people are satisfied and stunned.

beats.scene: Borgia and his advisers study a map of Tuscany marked with small flags
beats.summary: Chapter 7: Borgia plans to survive his father's death and to take Tuscany next.

beats.scene: A pope lies in a dim chamber while a young duke rests, ill, nearby
beats.summary: Chapter 7: in August 1503 Alexander dies while Borgia is gravely ill himself, with two enemy armies near.

beats.scene: Cardinals in red vote in a candlelit chapel while an old cardinal watches
beats.summary: Chapter 7: Borgia backs Giuliano della Rovere for pope, a man he had harmed, and so seals his own fall.

beats.scene: A duke in chains boards a ship under guard as a fleet watches
beats.summary: Chapter 7: Julius II turns on Borgia, who dies in 1507; Machiavelli still offers him as a model for those who rise by fortune.

beats.scene: Two roads: one through a dark alley, another towards a cheering crowd
beats.summary: Chapter 8: a man may also become prince by wicked deeds, or by the favour of his fellow citizens.

beats.scene: A young potter shapes clay at a wheel with a captain's cloak hanging nearby
beats.summary: Chapter 8: Agathocles, a potter's son, rises through the army to command in Syracuse.

beats.scene: A hall at dawn with guards at the doors and senators gathering
beats.summary: Chapter 8: Agathocles calls the senate and richest citizens together, has them killed, and rules without opposition.

beats.scene: Soldiers sail across a dark sea towards the African coast
beats.summary: Chapter 8: though twice beaten by Carthage and besieged, Agathocles carries the war to Africa and forces peace.

beats.scene: A king sits alone on a throne in a bare hall
beats.summary: Chapter 8: killing citizens, betraying friends and having no faith may win power, but not glory.

beats.scene: A young soldier in fine clothes rides back into his home town
beats.summary: Chapter 8: Oliverotto da Fermo, raised by his uncle and trained under the Vitelli, plans to seize his home town.

beats.scene: A grand banquet hall where armed men wait behind the curtains
beats.summary: Chapter 8: Oliverotto kills his uncle and the leading citizens at a banquet and rules Fermo, until Borgia has him strangled at Senigallia.

beats.scene: A ruler stands at a window, watching citizens go about their daily lives
beats.summary: Chapter 8: why do some cruel rulers stay safe while others fall? Cruelty can be well used or badly used.

beats.scene: Two clerks write in a ledger, one list shrinking and one growing
beats.summary: Chapter 8: cruelty is well used if done once for safety and then replaced by benefits, badly used if it grows with time.

beats.scene: A new ruler holds two scrolls, one of harsh orders and one of gifts
beats.summary: Chapter 8: injuries should be done all at once, benefits given little by little, and the ruler must not be changed by events.

beats.scene: A modest citizen is lifted up by cheering townspeople in a square
beats.summary: Chapter 9: a citizen can become prince by the favour of his fellow citizens, through fortunate cunning.

beats.scene: A street where workers stand on one side and rich nobles on the other
beats.summary: Chapter 9: every city holds two humours: the people do not want to be ruled or oppressed, and the great want to rule and oppress.

beats.scene: A prince sits among seated nobles who look as high as he does
beats.summary: Chapter 9: a prince raised by the great has trouble commanding his equals; one raised by the people stands alone.

beats.scene: A ruler gives a fair verdict while nobles frown and commoners nod
beats.summary: Chapter 9: the people are easier to satisfy, since they only want not to be oppressed; the worst they can do is desert him.

beats.scene: A ruler speaks kindly to a loyal noble while watching an ambitious one
beats.summary: Chapter 9: nobles who tie their fortunes to the prince should be honoured; those who hold back from ambition are dangerous.

beats.scene: A ruler walks among worried citizens inside a besieged city
beats.summary: Chapter 9: in adversity a prince needs the people friendly, as Nabis of Sparta did; the proverb about building on mud applies only to those who cannot command.

beats.scene: A commander with a full treasury reviews drilling troops on a wall
beats.summary: Chapter 10: a prince is strong if he can raise an army and meet attackers in the field; if he must hide behind walls, he is weak.

beats.scene: German free cities with thick walls, deep ditches and cannon on the towers
beats.summary: Chapter 10: the free cities of Germany obey the emperor when they like, and are so well fortified that nobody wants to attack them.

beats.scene: Public storehouses full of grain, barrels and firewood while workers are busy
beats.summary: Chapter 10: the cities keep a year's food, drink and fuel, give the poor work, and honour military training.

beats.scene: An army burns farms outside a walled city while citizens watch from the wall
beats.summary: Chapter 10: a prince with a strong city and a people who do not hate him is hard to attack, and burned houses bind citizens closer.

beats.scene: A pope in a tall hat blesses a crowd in a stone square
beats.summary: Chapter 11: Church states are won by ability or fortune but kept by neither; ancient religious customs hold them.

beats.scene: Peasants in the fields wave to a church banner beside a palace
beats.summary: Chapter 11: these rulers alone have states they need not defend and subjects they need not govern; Machiavelli will not discuss what God upholds.

beats.scene: A pope, a doge, a king and a duke sit around a table
beats.summary: Chapter 11: before 1494 five powers shared Italy, each watching the others.

beats.scene: Armed noblemen face each other in a Roman street while a pope watches
beats.summary: Chapter 11: the Orsini and Colonna families kept the papacy weak, and even bold Sixtus IV could not cure it.

beats.scene: A pope counts coins while armed soldiers wait at the door
beats.summary: Chapter 11: Alexander VI showed how much a pope could do with money and force, using Duke Valentino and the French invasion.

beats.scene: A pope looks proudly at a young duke while an old cardinal sighs
beats.summary: Chapter 11: Alexander wanted to make his son great, not the Church, but the Church inherited the result.

beats.scene: Pope Julius rides through a captured town with churchmen following
beats.summary: Chapter 11: Julius II finds the Church great, with the Romagna in hand and the barons crushed.

beats.scene: Julius II leads an army past a map marked with Bologna and Venice
beats.summary: Chapter 11: Julius sets out to win Bologna, crush the Venetians and drive out the French, and succeeds.

beats.scene: Two cardinals from rival families sit apart in a candlelit hall
beats.summary: Chapter 11: Julius kept the Orsini and Colonna quiet, since the Church was now strong and they had no cardinals of their own.

beats.scene: Pope Leo X reads in a quiet library of the Vatican
beats.summary: Chapter 11: Machiavelli hopes that Pope Leo X will make the Church great and venerable by goodness.

beats.scene: A scroll of laws on one table and a sword on another
beats.summary: Chapter 12: every state rests on good laws and good arms; hired and borrowed soldiers are useless and dangerous.

beats.scene: Soldiers at a camp fire count coins while one eyes the road
beats.summary: Chapter 12: hired soldiers fight only for a small wage, which is not enough to make them die for you.

beats.scene: A French king rides into Italy with a piece of chalk in his hand
beats.summary: Chapter 12: Italy's ruin came from hired soldiers; Charles VIII took Italy with chalk, and the real sins were the princes'.

beats.scene: A hired captain in fine armour stands before idle troops and an uneasy prince
beats.summary: Chapter 12: a hired captain is either excellent, so not to be trusted, or poor, so ruinous.

beats.scene: A prince in armour leads his own citizens while senators send a general
beats.summary: Chapter 12: a prince must lead his army himself and a republic must send its own citizens; Rome, Sparta and the Swiss stayed armed and free.

beats.scene: A general faces his own hired soldiers on a rocky hill
beats.summary: Chapter 12: Carthage was nearly crushed by its own hired soldiers, and Thebes lost its liberty to Philip of Macedon.

beats.scene: Crowds argue in a Milan street while a duke's funeral passes
beats.summary: Chapter 12: after Duke Filippo died, the Milanese hired Francesco Sforza, who joined their enemies and took the city.

beats.scene: Venetian ships at sea beside a land army losing a battle
beats.summary: Chapter 12: Venice was great with its own sailors, but hired captains on land led to the disaster at Vailà in 1509.

beats.scene: A Florentine council watches a hired English captain ride out of the city
beats.summary: Chapter 12: Florence also used hired captains, and was saved only because Hawkwood and Paolo Vitelli did not win too much.

beats.scene: A pope's soldiers and borrowed foreign troops march together to a siege
beats.summary: Chapter 13: borrowed soldiers help you only to harm you: if they lose you are ruined, if they win you are their prisoner.

beats.scene: French soldiers camp in a Tuscan field while Florentine officials watch, worried
beats.summary: Chapter 13: Florence borrowed French soldiers to take Pisa and was in more danger than ever; Constantinople's Turks never left.

beats.scene: A prince hands the keys of his city to a foreign captain
beats.summary: Chapter 13: borrowed arms are more dangerous than hired ones, because they are united and obey someone else.

beats.scene: Borgia reviews French knights, then Orsini horsemen, then his own soldiers
beats.summary: Chapter 13: Borgia used French, then Orsini, then his own arms, and his reputation grew each time.

beats.scene: A Syracusan captain gives a stern order to rows of hired soldiers
beats.summary: Chapter 13: Hiero of Syracuse saw that his hired soldiers were useless, and fought with his own men instead.

beats.scene: A young shepherd refuses a heavy suit of armour and holds a sling
beats.summary: Chapter 13: David refuses Saul's armour and takes his sling and knife; the arms of others fall off, weigh you down or bind you.

beats.scene: A French king reviews Swiss pikemen while his own foot soldiers stand aside
beats.summary: Chapter 13: Charles VII built his own army, but Louis XI hired Swiss troops; a state without its own arms is never secure.

beats.scene: A prince in plain armour studies a battle plan at a table
beats.summary: Chapter 14: a prince should think of nothing but war; Francesco Sforza rose by arms, and his sons fell by avoiding them.

beats.scene: A prince hunts through hills, noting rivers, marshes and slopes
beats.summary: Chapter 14: a prince should harden his body by hunting and learn the lie of the land, which teaches him his own country and every other.

beats.scene: Philopoemen rides with friends and draws a battle plan on the ground
beats.summary: Chapter 14: Philopoemen thought of war even in peace, and on country walks asked his friends how an army should act.

beats.scene: A prince reads a history book by lamplight beside a bust of Alexander
beats.summary: Chapter 14: a prince should read history and imitate a hero, as Alexander followed Achilles, and never be idle in peace.

beats.scene: A prince at a palace window looks out at a busy, untidy street
beats.summary: Chapter 15: Machiavelli will depart from other writers and describe the effective truth, not imagined republics.

beats.scene: A good-hearted man gives bread to a crowd while thieves slip behind him
beats.summary: Chapter 15: how people live is far from how they ought to live, and a man who is good in everything will be ruined among those who are not.

beats.scene: A scroll lists qualities: generous, mean, cruel, kind, faithful, false
beats.summary: Chapter 15: no prince can have every good quality, so he must avoid the vices that would lose his state.

beats.scene: A kind-looking ruler stands by an empty coin chest while a councillor worries
beats.summary: Chapter 15: something that looks like virtue may bring ruin, and something that looks like vice may bring safety.

beats.scene: A prince hands out jewels at a lavish feast while treasurers frown
beats.summary: Chapter 16: to be known as generous, a prince must spend without limit, then tax his people, and become hated and poor.

beats.scene: A thin, careful ruler counts his coins while a strong army drills behind him
beats.summary: Chapter 16: a prudent prince accepts the name of miser, because his thrift lets him defend the state without new taxes.

beats.scene: A pope, a French king and a Spanish king each hold a small purse
beats.summary: Chapter 16: in Machiavelli's time only rulers thought miserly did great things: Julius II, Louis XII and Ferdinand of Spain.

beats.scene: Julius Caesar stands before a cheering Roman crowd, scattering coins
beats.summary: Chapter 16: Caesar rose through generosity, but once in power would have ruined Rome by keeping it up.

beats.scene: A conqueror's army marches with loaded carts of plunder as soldiers cheer
beats.summary: Chapter 16: a prince who leads armies and lives on booty must give freely, and spending others' wealth adds to his reputation.

beats.scene: A candle burns down to its end beside an empty coin chest
beats.summary: Chapter 16: nothing consumes itself like generosity; a miser's name brings shame without hatred, a plunderer's with hatred.

beats.scene: A young duke sits in judgment in a calm town square among peaceful townspeople
beats.summary: Chapter 17: Borgia was called cruel, but his cruelty brought peace to the Romagna; Florence, to avoid seeming cruel, let Pistoia be ruined.

beats.scene: A magistrate orders a few punishments while a crowd looks on soberly
beats.summary: Chapter 17: a prince should not mind being called cruel if it keeps his subjects united; too much mercy lets disorder grow.

beats.scene: A ruler at a gate weighs a message in his hand while guards wait
beats.summary: Chapter 17: the prince must be slow to believe and to act, so that neither trust nor suspicion goes too far.

beats.scene: Two soldiers, one cheering a smiling prince and one saluting a stern prince
beats.summary: Chapter 17: is it better to be loved than feared? One would want both, but if one must be lacking, it is safer to be feared.

beats.scene: Citizens cheer a prince at the gate while others slip away behind him
beats.summary: Chapter 17: men are ungrateful, fickle and greedy; while you benefit them they are yours, but when need comes near they turn away.

beats.scene: A chain of gold links breaks while a stone wall stands firm
beats.summary: Chapter 17: bought friendships cannot be spent in need; love is a chain broken by self-interest, fear a dread that never leaves.

beats.scene: A stern ruler hands a farmer his land deed back before a small house
beats.summary: Chapter 17: the prince should be feared but not hated, keeping away from his subjects' property and women; men forget a father's death sooner than a lost inheritance.

beats.scene: A general leads a mixed army of many races through mountain snow
beats.summary: Chapter 17: with an army, a prince must not mind being called cruel; Hannibal's army of many nations never quarrelled.

beats.scene: A Roman general in a camp tent while soldiers murmur outside
beats.summary: Chapter 17: Scipio's too-gentle rule led to a mutiny in Spain; his soft nature was hidden because he lived under the Senate.

beats.scene: A prince stands between a loving crowd, a fearful crowd and an empty chair
beats.summary: Chapter 17: men love as they please and fear as the prince pleases, so a wise prince builds on what is his own and avoids hatred.

beats.scene: A prince shakes hands honestly while a rival hides a trick behind his back
beats.summary: Chapter 18: everyone praises a prince who keeps his word, yet the princes who did great things cared little for promises.

beats.scene: A centaur teaches a young prince in a forest glade
beats.summary: Chapter 18: there are two ways to fight, with laws and with force; the story of Chiron the centaur shows that a prince must know both.

beats.scene: A fox and a lion walk side by side beneath a prince's banner
beats.summary: Chapter 18: a prince must be a fox to recognise traps and a lion to frighten wolves.

beats.scene: A prince tears up a treaty while a messenger watches
beats.summary: Chapter 18: a prudent ruler cannot keep faith when it harms him; if all men were good this would be wrong, but they are not.

beats.scene: A smiling prince bows politely with a hidden letter in his sleeve
beats.summary: Chapter 18: the fox must hide his nature and be a great pretender, because men are so simple that a deceiver always finds someone to deceive.

beats.scene: A pope in rich robes swears an oath, hand raised, as a messenger waits
beats.summary: Chapter 18: Alexander VI thought of nothing but deceiving men, swore the greatest oaths and kept them least, and always succeeded.

beats.scene: A prince in a mirror shows a kind face over a cold stare
beats.summary: Chapter 18: a prince need not have all the good qualities but must seem to; his mind must be ready to turn when necessity demands.

beats.scene: A prince speaks from a pulpit beside banners of mercy, faith, honesty and religion
beats.summary: Chapter 18: every word must seem full of mercy, faith, honesty, humanity and religion, and the last is the most necessary to seem to have.

beats.scene: A crowd watches a king's procession while a few at the edge look closer
beats.summary: Chapter 18: people judge more by eyes than by hands; everyone sees what you seem, few know what you are, and in princes one looks to the result.

beats.scene: A smiling ruler preaches peace from a pulpit while soldiers march behind him
beats.summary: Chapter 18: a certain prince of present times, whom it is not good to name, preaches only peace and faith, though he is an enemy of both.

beats.scene: A prince walks past plain citizens, some of whom look angry
beats.summary: Chapter 19: a prince must avoid being hated, by taking property and women, and being despised, by seeming weak or changeable.

beats.scene: A watchtower with a loyal army and friends gathered at the gate
beats.summary: Chapter 19: a respected prince is hard to attack; he has two fears, subjects at home and powers abroad, and answers the second with good arms and friends.

beats.scene: A prince among cheering citizens while a hooded plotter hesitates in the shadows
beats.summary: Chapter 19: the best remedy against conspiracies is not to be hated by the people; plotters have only fear, while the prince has law, friends and goodwill.

beats.scene: A baby heir is carried through a Bologna street as a crowd rises
beats.summary: Chapter 19: when the Canneschi killed Annibale Bentivoglio, the people of Bologna killed the plotters and fetched another Bentivoglio from Florence.

beats.scene: A judge in a French court sits between a king and his nobles
beats.summary: Chapter 19: the French Parlement acts as a third judge between king, nobles and people; princes should leave unpopular tasks to others.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers demand pay from an emperor while a crowd waits outside
beats.summary: Chapter 19: the Roman emperors faced a third difficulty, the cruelty and greed of their soldiers, while the people wanted quiet.

beats.scene: A philosopher emperor in a plain robe, honoured, beside two fallen rulers
beats.summary: Chapter 19: Marcus died honoured; Pertinax was ruined within months for making soldiers live honestly; Alexander Severus was despised as ruled by his mother.

beats.scene: An emperor in a lion-skin cloak and a fox-fur cap stands before soldiers
beats.summary: Chapter 19: Septimius Severus, a lion and a fox, marched on Rome to avenge Pertinax, defeated Niger and tricked Albinus.

beats.scene: Three emperors' thrones, each with a dagger lying near it
beats.summary: Chapter 19: Caracalla, Commodus and Maximinus were ruined by cruelty, contempt and low birth.

beats.scene: A modern prince at a desk compares two portraits, of Marcus and of Severus
beats.summary: Chapter 19: modern princes must please the people more than soldiers, except the Turk and the Sultan; a new prince takes from Severus to found a state and from Marcus to keep it.

beats.scene: A new prince hands weapons to villagers outside a newly taken town
beats.summary: Chapter 20: a new prince never disarms his subjects but arms them, so their weapons become his and the doubtful become loyal.

beats.scene: A city divided by a street barrier, with soldiers waiting nearby
beats.summary: Chapter 20: holding cities by dividing their people once seemed wise, but divided cities fall quickly to an enemy, as Venice found after Vailà.

beats.scene: A prince climbs a ladder built from his enemies' weapons
beats.summary: Chapter 20: Fortune makes enemies for a new prince so he can climb higher; former enemies often serve better than early friends.

beats.scene: A mighty castle looms over a town whose people look up with fear
beats.summary: Chapter 20: fortresses are useful or not according to the times; Vitelli and Guido Ubaldo tore theirs down, and the Sforza castle in Milan brought endless trouble.

beats.scene: A countess stands before the walls of her fortress as soldiers approach
beats.summary: Chapter 20: the best fortress is not to be hated by the people; the Countess of Forlì was helped once by her fortress, but not when Borgia attacked.

beats.scene: A king in armour leads a great army towards the mountains of Granada
beats.summary: Chapter 21: nothing makes a prince esteemed like great undertakings; Ferdinand of Aragon began with the war on Granada, which kept his barons busy.

beats.scene: Soldiers and priests march along a Spanish road towards distant ships
beats.summary: Chapter 21: Ferdinand drove Jews and converted Jews from Spain under cover of religion, then attacked Africa, Italy and France, never giving men time to plot.

beats.scene: A neutral ruler stands alone between two armies as both turn away
beats.summary: Chapter 21: a prince is esteemed when he is a true friend or true enemy; neutrality leaves him prey to the winner, as Antiochus and the Achaeans learned.

beats.scene: A smaller prince shakes hands with a stronger one over a map
beats.summary: Chapter 21: joining the winner makes him owe you, joining the loser gets you shelter; never ally with a stronger prince unless forced; choose the lesser evil.

beats.scene: Craftsmen and farmers work peacefully while festival banners hang over a town square
beats.summary: Chapter 21: a prince should honour talent, let citizens trade and farm without fear, reward those who enlarge the state, and hold festivals.

beats.scene: A prince sits among his ministers while a visitor studies their faces
beats.summary: Chapter 22: the choice of ministers shows a prince's wisdom, as Antonio da Venafro showed Pandolfo Petrucci's.

beats.scene: Three men: one draws up a plan, one judges it, and one stares blankly
beats.summary: Chapter 22: there are three kinds of brains: one understands alone, one understands what others show, one neither; a prince must at least be the second.

beats.scene: A minister counts his own coins while his prince watches
beats.summary: Chapter 22: a minister who thinks more of himself than of the prince can never be trusted; the prince must honour and enrich a good one.

beats.scene: A courtier whispers praise into a prince's ear in a gilded room
beats.summary: Chapter 23: courts are full of flatterers; the only defence is to let men know the truth will not offend you, but then you risk losing respect.

beats.scene: A prince sits with three grey-haired advisers who speak only when asked
beats.summary: Chapter 23: a wise prince chooses a few wise men, lets only them speak the truth, asks about everything, then decides himself and holds firm.

beats.scene: An emperor writes secret orders while courtiers whisper and change his mind
beats.summary: Chapter 23: Emperor Maximilian took no advice yet was talked out of his plans; good counsel must come from the prince's own prudence.

beats.scene: A new prince on a fresh throne is cheered; an old king is forgotten
beats.summary: Chapter 24: a new prince who follows this advice seems like an old one, and earns double glory for founding and strengthening a state.

beats.scene: A map of Italy with dark patches where princely states have fallen
beats.summary: Chapter 24: the Italian princes who lost their states shared the same faults: poor arms, and a hostile people or unsecured nobles.

beats.scene: A king of Macedon stands on a hill fort holding off a Roman army
beats.summary: Chapter 24: Philip of Macedon, a soldier who kept the people content and the nobles secure, fought Rome for years and kept his kingdom.

beats.scene: An empty palace hall at dusk; a lone prince stares at a distant road
beats.summary: Chapter 24: fallen princes should blame their idleness, not Fortune; only defences that depend on yourself are good, certain and lasting.

beats.scene: A sailor lets his boat drift on a stormy sea, hands off the oar
beats.summary: Chapter 25: many believe Fortune and God govern everything and human prudence is useless; Machiavelli admits he has sometimes leaned that way.

beats.scene: A balance scale: half filled with chance, half with human choice
beats.summary: Chapter 25: so that free will is not lost, fortune is judged the arbiter of half our actions, leaving the other half to us.

beats.scene: A wild river bursts its banks across a green valley as villagers run
beats.summary: Chapter 25: fortune is like a violent river that floods the plains, tears down trees and houses, and cannot be resisted while it rages.

beats.scene: Villagers build dikes and channels beside a calm river in dry weather
beats.summary: Chapter 25: in quiet times men can build dikes and banks; fortune shows her power where no virtue has prepared to resist her.

beats.scene: A field without dikes as a flood pours across a map of Italy
beats.summary: Chapter 25: Italy is a country without dikes; if it had been defended like Germany, Spain and France, the flood would have done far less harm.

beats.scene: A prince smiles on a throne, then stands alone and ruined
beats.summary: Chapter 25: a prince may be happy today and ruined tomorrow without changing; he who relies wholly on fortune falls when it turns, and happy is he whose way suits the times.

beats.scene: Two travellers choose different roads, one cautious and one bold
beats.summary: Chapter 25: men chase glory and riches by different means; two methods can succeed, and two similar ones can fail, depending on the times.

beats.scene: A cautious man waits at a rising river while a bold man crosses
beats.summary: Chapter 25: a cautious man does not know how to be bold when times demand it, and nobody is wise enough to change his nature.

beats.scene: A fierce old pope on horseback leads soldiers out of Rome
beats.summary: Chapter 25: Julius II acted impetuously, and at Bologna his bold move froze Spain and Venice and drew France after him.

beats.scene: A young horseman charges a stormy sea; an old man hesitates ashore
beats.summary: Chapter 25: Julius died before the times changed; Machiavelli judges boldness better than caution, since Fortune, he says, favours the young.

beats.scene: Machiavelli at his desk with a map of Italy spread before him
beats.summary: Chapter 26: Machiavelli asks whether the times in Italy are right for a new prince, and decides that many things point the same way.

beats.scene: Chained figures in a ruined Italian landscape beside a broken column
beats.summary: Chapter 26: as Israel had to be enslaved for Moses, Italy has been brought low: more enslaved than the Hebrews, more scattered than the Athenians, without a head.

beats.scene: Italy as a wounded woman kneels and raises a banner with open hands
beats.summary: Chapter 26: a spark appeared in one man but fortune rejected him; Italy awaits a redeemer and would follow any banner, and the house of Medici is her best hope.

beats.scene: A sea parts, a cloud leads the way, and manna falls in a field
beats.summary: Chapter 26: the great founders were only men with smaller chances; war is just for those to whom it is necessary; God will not do everything.

beats.scene: Two champions fight a duel while a ragged army behind them scatters
beats.summary: Chapter 26: Italians are strong in duels but weak in armies, because their leaders are weak; the list of failed battles.

beats.scene: A prince inspects ranks of Italian foot soldiers drilling in the sun
beats.summary: Chapter 26: the Medici must provide arms of their own; Swiss and Spanish infantry have weaknesses that a new kind of army could use, as at Ravenna.

beats.scene: Crowds welcome a liberator at every gate with tears and flowers
beats.summary: Chapter 26: a liberator would be welcomed with love and tears in every province; the book ends with Petrarch's lines that courage will take up arms.

beats.scene: A young nobleman sets a rolled manuscript aside while hunting dogs wait
beats.summary: Afterwards: the Medici give Machiavelli no post, the call to free Italy goes unanswered, and Lorenzo dies in 1519.

beats.scene: Machiavelli at a desk with a stack of manuscripts: play, treatise, history
beats.summary: Afterwards: he writes the Discourses on Livy, the comedy Mandragola and The Art of War.

beats.scene: Machiavelli kneels before a Medici pope, presenting a heavy book
beats.summary: Afterwards: in 1520 Cardinal Giulio de' Medici asks him to write a history of Florence, which he presents to Pope Clement VII in 1526.

beats.scene: A stone tomb in Santa Croce with a marble figure and a Latin inscription
beats.summary: Afterwards: in 1527 Rome is sacked and the Medici expelled, Machiavelli is passed over, and dies on 21 June aged 58; his tomb in Santa Croce is later inscribed.

beats.scene: A printer's workshop in Rome, with pages hanging to dry beside a wooden press
beats.summary: Afterwards: The Prince passes from hand to hand in copies and is first printed in Rome and Florence in 1532.

beats.scene: A stern cardinal places a book on a list of forbidden books
beats.summary: Afterwards: Cardinal Pole says the book seems written by Satan's hand, and in 1559 the Church bans all of Machiavelli's works.

beats.scene: A stage villain in black holds a dagger and a book
beats.summary: Afterwards: Elizabethan playwrights wrote 'Machiavels' as scheming villains, and 'Machiavellian' came to mean cunning and ruthless.

beats.scene: A young king writes at a desk while soldiers cross a snowy border
beats.summary: Afterwards: Frederick of Prussia's Anti-Machiavel (1740), edited by Voltaire, urged honest rule, yet within months he invaded Silesia.

beats.scene: A French thinker writes at a desk while Italian patriots wave flags outside
beats.summary: Afterwards: Rousseau read the book as a secret lesson for the people, and Italian patriots read its last chapter as a call for unity.

beats.scene: Two Italian words, virtù and fortuna, on a page beside a coin
beats.summary: Afterwards: virtù means skill, energy and courage rather than goodness; fortuna means luck; the saying that the end justifies the means is not in the book.

beats.scene: Three readers around a table, each holding a different edition and arguing
beats.summary: Afterwards: scholars still disagree whether The Prince is honest advice, a warning to peoples, a satire, or a clever job application.

beats.scene: A modern manager reads The Prince at a desk with a notebook
beats.summary: Afterwards: modern readers can take from it foresight, good advisers and own strength, while treating its advice on cruelty and deceit as history.

beats.scene: A modern reader closes The Prince on a desk beside a notebook
beats.summary: Conclusion: a modern reader can learn foresight and how power works, and must decide for themselves how far good aims excuse hard means.

He rode on long journeys to speak with kings and popes.
In 1502 he spent weeks with Cesare Borgia and watched him closely.
He trained Florence's own men to fight, instead of paying hired soldiers.
In 1512 Spanish soldiers took Prato, and the Florentine army ran away.
In November 1512 the Medici took away his job.
In 1513 he was put in jail, but he said he knew nothing.
After that he moved his family to a small farm near Florence.
By day he cut wood and played cards with the village men.
At night he put on fine clothes and read old books.
He wanted to give his book to the young Lorenzo de' Medici.
He said his best gift was everything he had learned.
A painter of mountains must stand in the valley below.
He asked Lorenzo to look down and see his bad luck.

Settlers cost little, but soldiers cost a great deal.

The Romans saw trouble early and fought it far from Italy.

Rome destroyed three cities and never lost them again.
A city that once was free never forgets its freedom.
People used to a prince will obey a new ruler more easily.
Archers aim high to hit a target that is far away.
Moses found a people who wanted to escape slavery.
Romulus and Theseus also used a chance that came to them.
New ways are hard to start, because old ways have friends.
A reformer who must beg for help usually fails.
People change their minds, so a founder needs real strength.
Savonarola lost power when the people stopped believing him.
Hiero was an ordinary man who became ruler of Syracuse.
A ruler who gets power by luck often cannot keep it.
Francesco Sforza earned his power, but Cesare Borgia was given his.
Pope Alexander VI wanted to make his son a great ruler.
He helped the French king, and the French helped his son.
Borgia won the Romagna, but he did not trust his soldiers.
Borgia invited his rebel captains to meet him, and trapped them.
The Romagna was full of thieves, so Borgia sent a hard governor.
Borgia then had the harsh governor killed, to please the people.
Borgia planned to conquer Tuscany, and Florence had reason to fear.
Pope Alexander died in 1503, and Borgia was very sick too.
Borgia helped the wrong man to become pope and was ruined.
Machiavelli thought new rulers should learn from Borgia's example.
A man can also become a ruler by crime or by popular favour.
Agathocles was a potter's son who joined the army.

He sailed to Africa and forced Carthage to make peace.
He won power, but he did not win true glory.
Oliverotto was a young soldier who wanted to rule his home town.
He killed his uncle at a feast and took the town.
Some rulers stay safe after cruel acts, but others do not.
Cruel acts should be done once, not again and again.
Do hard things at once, and be kind little by little.
A citizen can become prince if his fellow citizens support him.
In every city the people and the nobles want different things.
Nobles who raise a prince may think they are his equals.
The people only want safety, but the great want power.
A ruler should honour loyal nobles and watch the ambitious ones.
A ruler without the people's support has no help in danger.
A strong ruler can raise an army and fight his enemies.
German cities had strong walls, so enemies left them alone.
The cities stored food for a year and gave work to the poor.
A strong city and a loyal people can stop any army.
Church lands are kept by old customs of faith.
People stayed loyal to Church rulers, even when badly governed.
Before 1494 five powers shared Italy and watched each other.
Two noble families in Rome kept the pope weak.
Alexander VI showed how much a pope could do with money.
He worked for his son, but the Church gained most.
Julius II found the Church already great and strong.
Julius won Bologna and fought the French and other enemies.
Julius also kept the Roman families quiet and under control.
Machiavelli hoped Pope Leo X would make the Church great.
Good laws and good soldiers are the basis of every state.
Hired soldiers fight for pay and run away from danger.
In 1494 the French king took Italy almost without a fight.
A good hired captain wants power for himself, not for you.
Rome and Sparta stayed free for centuries with their own soldiers.
Carthage and Thebes both suffered from the soldiers they hired.
Milan hired Francesco Sforza, and he took the city himself.
Venice lost in one day what had taken it centuries to win.
Florence also hired captains, and it feared what they might do.
Borrowed soldiers help you only to harm you later.
Turkish soldiers came to help Greece, but they never left.
Borrowed armies are more dangerous than hired ones.
Borgia used French, then hired, then his own soldiers.
Hiero found hired soldiers useless, so he used his own.
David refused Saul's heavy armour and took his sling.
A ruler without his own army is never truly safe.
A ruler must always study war, even in times of peace.
A ruler should hunt often and learn the shape of the land.
Philopoemen made his friends plan battles during country walks.
A wise ruler reads history and copies great men.
Machiavelli says he will write about real life, not dreams.
A man who is always good will fail among bad men.
No ruler can have every good quality, so he must choose.
Some virtues can ruin a ruler, and some faults can save him.
A ruler who gives too much will soon have to tax everyone.
A careful ruler may be called mean, but he stays safe.
Great deeds in our time were done by careful rulers.
Generosity helps a man rise, but it harms a ruler.
A conqueror may give away what he has taken from enemies.
Giving too much leaves a ruler poor, and then he is despised.
Borgia was called cruel, but he brought peace to his lands.
Too much mercy lets crime grow and hurts the whole state.
A ruler should not trust too quickly or fear too much.
A ruler would like both love and fear, but must choose.
People help you when you are strong, but not in danger.
Friends you buy with money will leave when you need them.
A ruler must never take his people's land or goods.
Hannibal led soldiers from many lands, and they never argued.
Scipio was too kind to his soldiers, and they rebelled.
People love as they wish, but they fear as the ruler wishes.
We praise honest rulers, but many great rulers were not honest.
A ruler must act like a man, and sometimes like a beast.
A ruler needs the cunning of a fox and the strength of a lion.
A clever ruler breaks a promise when it harms him.
People are simple, so a clever liar finds victims easily.
Pope Alexander VI broke his promises, but people still believed him.
A ruler should seem good, but be ready to act otherwise.
A ruler should always sound kind, honest and religious.
People judge by what they see, not by what is true.
One king speaks only of peace, but he is its enemy.
A ruler must avoid being hated and avoid being despised.
With strong arms, a ruler will also have strong friends.
A ruler loved by his people is safe from plots.
The people of Bologna took revenge for their murdered ruler.
A ruler should let others do the unpopular jobs.
Roman emperors had to please soldiers and the people.
Marcus Aurelius was respected, but Pertinax was killed quickly.
Severus tricked one rival and then defeated another.
Cruel emperors were hated, and their own men killed them.
A new ruler should learn from Severus, then from Marcus.
A new ruler should arm his people, not take their weapons.
Dividing a city's people did not save Venice.
Old enemies can sometimes become a ruler's most faithful helpers.
Strong castles can help a ruler, but they can also harm him.
The best castle is a people who do not hate you.
King Ferdinand won fame by starting great wars.
Ferdinand fought war after war, so nobody could plot.
A ruler who stays neutral will be crushed by the winner.
A ruler who joins a winner is owed some thanks.
A good ruler protects trade and holds festivals for the people.
A ruler is judged by the people he chooses to help him.
Some minds find answers, some judge them, and some do neither.
A good helper thinks of his master, not only of himself.
Courts are full of flatterers who tell rulers what they want.
A wise ruler asks a few wise people for the truth.
A ruler should ask for advice when he wants it.
A new ruler who rules well soon seems like an old one.
Italian princes lost their lands because they had weak armies.
Philip of Macedon fought Rome for years and kept his kingdom.
Only defences you build yourself will save you in bad times.
Some people think luck decides everything, so trying is useless.
Luck rules about half of our lives, and we rule the rest.
Fortune is like a river that floods and breaks everything.

Italy had no walls against the flood, so it was ruined.
A ruler can fall without changing; only the times changed.
Different methods can win, and the same method can fail.
A careful man fails when the times ask for courage.
Pope Julius acted fast and boldly, and it worked.
Machiavelli says bold people often do better than careful ones.

Italy waits for a leader to heal her wounds.
God will not do everything, so people must act.
Italians fought well alone, but badly in armies.
A new ruler must first build an army of his own people.
The book ends with a hope that Italy will be free.

He wrote plays and books about government and war.
In 1520 a Medici cardinal asked him to write a history.
He died in 1527, aged fifty-eight, and lies in Florence.
The Prince was printed in 1532, five years after he died.
The Church banned his books in 1559 as dangerous.
On stage, cunning villains were often called Machiavels.

B1B2: In 1498 Machiavelli became a senior clerk of the republic of Florence, at the age of only twenty-nine. He was not a nobleman, but his quick mind and clear writing soon made him useful to the city's leaders.
As a diplomat he travelled many times to the court of King Louis XII of France. He also visited the pope and the German emperor, and he wrote long reports on everything he saw.

In 1502 Florence sent Machiavelli to the camp of Cesare Borgia, a young conqueror who was frightening all of Italy. For several months he watched how Borgia planned and decided, and he wrote home about it often.

Machiavelli believed that a state should defend itself with its own citizens, not with hired soldiers. In 1506 he helped to set up a militia for Florence, and in 1509 it helped to win back the city of Pisa.

In August 1512 a Spanish army broke into the town of Prato, and Machiavelli's militia ran away. A few days later the head of the republic, Piero Soderini, left Florence, and the Medici family came back.
In November 1512 the new rulers dismissed Machiavelli from every office he held. He was also forbidden to enter the government palace, where he had worked for fourteen years.
In February 1513 his name was found on a list kept by men who plotted against the Medici. He was arrested and questioned under torture, but he said he knew nothing, and in March he was set free.
After prison Machiavelli left Florence and went to live on a small farm that his family owned. It stood near the village of Sant'Andrea, among woods and fields, some miles south of the city.
In the mornings he walked in the woods and watched his men cut trees. In the afternoons he sat at the inn, playing cards with a butcher, a miller and two kiln workers, and quarrelling over pennies.

When evening came he took off his muddy farm clothes and put on the robes he had worn at court. Dressed like that, he sat with the writers of ancient Rome and Greece, and out of those talks came a short book about princes.
Machiavelli dedicated his little book to Lorenzo de' Medici, a young ruler of the family that now governed Florence. He hoped that a gift from a poor man might win him a place in the new government.

In the dedication he says he has nothing more valuable to give than his knowledge of the deeds of great men. He learned it, he says, from long experience of modern events and from constant reading about the ancient world.

Machiavelli compares himself to a painter of landscapes, who stands in the valley to study the mountains. In the same way, he says, a man of the people may understand princes well, even though he is not one.
Machiavelli ends the dedication with a request that Lorenzo will look down from his high place and notice a man who has suffered. He says he has been treated cruelly by a long run of bad luck.
Machiavelli starts by saying that every state is either a republic or a principality. A principality is a state ruled by one prince, and it is the only kind that this book will discuss.
Principalities are either old, handed down from father to son, or new. A new one may be made from nothing, or it may be joined to a prince's old lands, as Naples was to Spain.

Machiavelli says that a state ruled by one family for a long time is the easiest kind to keep. People are used to the family, so the prince only needs to keep the old customs and act wisely when trouble comes.
Machiavelli gives an example from his own times, the Duke of Ferrara. He held out against the Venetians in 1484 and against Pope Julius II in 1510 only because his family had ruled there for so long.
A prince born to rule has less reason to offend his people, so he is naturally better loved. Unless he has some very bad habit, his subjects will usually be fond of him.

Machiavelli adds that the memory of old changes fades when a family rules for a long time. He compares a change to the rough edge of a wall, because one change always leaves a place where the next one can be built.
In a state joined to another, people often welcome a new ruler because they hope for a better life. They take up arms against the old one, but they are soon disappointed.
A conqueror has to hurt many of his new subjects, by housing soldiers among them and by other injuries that follow conquest. He also cannot reward the people who helped him as much as they hoped.
A rebel country is harder to lose once it has been conquered a second time. The ruler can punish the guilty, remove the doubtful and strengthen his weak points.
If a new land has the same language and customs as the old one, it is easy to keep. France held Burgundy, Brittany, Gascony and Normandy for a long time in this way.
When the language, customs and laws are different, it is hard to hold a new land. The best remedy is for the new ruler to go and live there himself, as the Turk did in Greece.
The second remedy is to send colonies, which are groups of settlers, to one or two key places. They cost little and hurt only a few, while an army of occupation costs far more and angers everyone.
A prince who holds such a land should become the leader and protector of the weaker neighbours. He should weaken the strong ones and never let a powerful foreigner enter the country.
The Romans saw trouble coming from far away and dealt with it quickly. They preferred to fight Philip and Antiochus in Greece rather than wait for them in Italy.
Doctors say that a wasting fever is easy to cure but hard to spot at the start. Later it is easy to spot and almost impossible to cure, and the same is true of trouble in a state.

Louis XII of France made five mistakes in Italy, and so he soon lost what he had won. When a French cardinal said that Italians knew nothing of war, Machiavelli replied that the French knew nothing of government.
Alexander the Great conquered the huge empire of King Darius in only a few years, and then he died. His generals kept it, though, and the people did not rise against them.
Machiavelli says there are two ways to govern a state. In Turkey the ruler's servants govern by his favour, while in France the barons hold their own lands and have their own followers.
It is very hard to conquer a ruler like the Turk, because his servants are loyal to him alone and cannot easily be bribed. But once he is beaten in the field, only his own family is left to fear.

A kingdom like France is easy to enter, because some barons are always unhappy and will help a stranger. It is much harder to keep, because the conqueror can neither satisfy the barons nor remove them all.

Darius ruled like the Turk, so Alexander had only to defeat him, and his heirs kept the empire in peace. The Romans were not so lucky in Spain, Gaul and Greece, where the many small states rebelled again and again.
Machiavelli names three ways to hold a city that is used to its own laws and freedom. A conqueror can destroy it, go and live there, or let it keep its laws while a few friends govern it for him.
The Spartans held Athens and Thebes by setting up governments of a few friends in each city. Even so, they lost both cities in the end.
The Romans destroyed Capua, Carthage and Numantia, and they never lost those places. In Greece they tried to leave the cities free, but it failed, and in the end they had to destroy many of them.
A city used to freedom will always remember the name of liberty and its old laws. Pisa, which had been under the rule of Florence for nearly a hundred years, rose up the moment a chance appeared.

Where people are used to a prince and his family has ended, they find it hard to choose a new ruler from among themselves. Republics are far more dangerous, because their hatred and desire for revenge never rest.
Machiavelli says that people usually follow roads that others have made. A wise ruler copies great men, and like a good archer he aims above the target so that his arrow will reach it.

Machiavelli says the great founders owed fortune only the opportunity, and the rest was their own skill. Moses found the Israelites slaves in Egypt and ready to follow him, and Cyrus found the Persians unhappy under the Medes.
In the old stories, Romulus was left to die as a baby and could not stay in Alba, so he founded Rome. Theseus found the Athenians scattered, and he joined them together as one people in Athens.

Machiavelli says nothing is harder to manage than introducing a new order of things. Everyone who gains from the old order becomes his enemy, and those who might gain from the new give only lukewarm support.
Machiavelli asks whether a new ruler stands on his own or depends on others. If he has to beg for help, he usually fails, but if he can use force, he is rarely in danger.
Machiavelli says that every armed prophet has won and every unarmed one has failed. People are easy to persuade but hard to keep persuaded, so a founder must be able to make them believe by force.
In Machiavelli's own times, a preacher called Savonarola led Florence for a few years. When the crowd stopped believing him, he had no force to hold them, and in 1498 he was put to death.

Machiavelli adds a smaller example, Hiero of Syracuse, who rose from being a private citizen to being the prince of his city. Fortune gave him only a chance, and he worked hard to win power but little to keep it.
Chapter seven is about those who become rulers by good luck or by the help of others. They reach the top without effort, as if they could fly, but all their troubles begin once they get there.

Machiavelli gives two examples from recent times, one of skill and one of luck. Francesco Sforza became Duke of Milan by his own ability, but Cesare Borgia gained his state through his father's luck and lost it.

Pope Alexander VI wanted to make his son Cesare a ruler, but he had many problems. The only lands he could give him belonged to the Church, and the Venetians and the Duke of Milan would not allow that.
In 1498 the pope helped King Louis XII of France to cancel his marriage. In return, the French king sent soldiers to help Cesare Borgia win lands in the Romagna.
With French help, Borgia won the Romagna, a large region of towns and farms in central Italy. But he could not trust the Orsini soldiers who fought for him, and he was afraid of the French king.

Borgia pretended to forgive the Orsini and the other captains who had turned against him, and he invited them to a meeting at Senigallia. There, on the last day of 1502, he had them seized, and two of them were put to death the same night.
The Romagna had been badly ruled by weak lords and was full of thieves and quarrels. Borgia sent a harsh and quick governor, Remirro de Orco, and gave him full power to bring order.

Borgia feared that people would hate the harsh governor's methods, so he set up a fair court in the region. Then he had Remirro put to death in the square at Cesena, to show that the cruelty had not been his own idea.

Borgia made careful plans to stay safe after his father's death, and he had already carried out most of them. He also meant to conquer Tuscany, and Machiavelli notes that Florence would then have had no remedy.
In August 1503 Pope Alexander VI died, just when Borgia himself lay seriously ill. His new state was far from safe, with two strong enemy armies close by.

When the new pope had to be chosen, Borgia backed Giuliano della Rovere, a cardinal he had once harmed. Machiavelli says this was his fatal mistake, because great men do not forget old injuries when they receive new favours.

Pope Julius II soon turned against Borgia, who lost his lands and died in a small battle in Spain in 1507. Machiavelli still holds him up as a model for those who rise by luck, and he blames only his choice of pope.
Chapter eight describes two more ways to become a prince. One is through wicked and criminal acts, and the other is through the favour of one's fellow citizens.
Agathocles was the son of a potter in Sicily, and his early life was wicked. But he was strong and brave, and he rose through the army until he became a leading officer in Syracuse.

One morning Agathocles called the senate and the richest citizens together, as if to talk about the city's business. At a signal his soldiers killed them all, and he took power without any open opposition.
Carthage twice defeated Agathocles and then besieged his city. He left part of his army to defend it, sailed to Africa with the rest, and forced the Carthaginians to make peace.
Machiavelli admits that Agathocles showed great courage and skill in danger. But killing citizens, betraying friends and having no faith or pity may win power, he says, but never glory.
Oliverotto da Fermo was raised by his uncle and trained as a soldier under the Vitelli family. He grew skilled and ambitious, and he decided that he wanted to rule his home town of Fermo.
Oliverotto came home with a hundred horsemen and held a grand banquet for his uncle and the leading men of Fermo. His soldiers killed them all, and he made himself the ruler of the town.
Machiavelli asks why some cruel rulers, like Agathocles, stayed safe for a long time while others fell quickly. His answer is that cruelty can be well used or badly used.
A cruel act is well used if it is done once, out of need, and then stopped and replaced by kindness. It is badly used if it begins small and grows worse with time.
Machiavelli says a conqueror should do all his harsh acts at once, so that people feel them less. Kindnesses, on the other hand, should be given slowly, so that people enjoy them for longer.

A civil principality is one where a citizen becomes prince by the favour of his fellow citizens, without crime or great violence. He needs neither great luck nor great strength, Machiavelli says, but a fortunate kind of cleverness.
Machiavelli says every city holds two groups with different desires. The people do not want to be ruled or crushed by the great, and the great want to rule and crush the people.
A prince raised by the great has trouble, because he is surrounded by men who think they are his equals. A prince raised by the people stands alone, with almost nobody around him who refuses to obey.
The people want only not to be oppressed, so they are easier to satisfy than the great, who want to rule. A prince can also live without particular nobles, but he can never do without his people.
Machiavelli says the nobles can be sorted into two main kinds. Those who tie their fortunes to the prince should be honoured, but those who hold back from ambition should be watched like enemies.
A prince must keep the people friendly, or he has no remedy when trouble comes. Nabis of Sparta held out against all Greece and a Roman army because his people stood behind him.
Machiavelli asks whether a prince can defend himself alone or must always depend on others. A prince with enough men and money to raise an army is strong, but one who must hide behind walls is weak.
The free cities of Germany obeyed the emperor only when they wanted to. Their walls and ditches were so strong that nobody wished to attack them.
The German cities stored enough food, drink and fuel to last a year. They also gave the poor work in the trades that kept the city alive, and they trained their citizens in the use of arms.

A prince with a strong city and a people who do not hate him is very hard to attack. Even if the enemy burns the fields, the citizens often stand closer to the prince, because they have suffered in his defence.

Chapter eleven is about the lands of the Church, which are ruled by popes and bishops. They are won by skill or luck, but they are kept by old customs of religion that protect their rulers whatever they do.

Machiavelli says these rulers alone have states they do not need to defend and subjects they do not need to govern. Because higher causes support them, he says, it would be foolish of him to discuss them further.

Before the French king Charles VIII arrived in 1494, five powers shared Italy. They were the pope, the Venetians, the King of Naples, the Duke of Milan and the Florentines, and each watched the others carefully.
The Orsini and Colonna families of Rome were always quarrelling, and they stood armed under the pope's eyes. This kept the papacy weak, and even a bold pope like Sixtus IV could not cure it.
Alexander VI showed better than any pope before him what money and armed force could do. He used his son Cesare as his tool, and he took advantage of the French invasion.
Alexander's aim was to make his son great, not the Church. But when the duke fell, it was the Church that inherited the result of all that work.
Julius II became pope after Alexander and found the Church already great. It held the whole Romagna, the Roman barons were broken, and there were new ways to raise money.

Julius set out to win Bologna, to crush the Venetians and to drive the French out of Italy. All of these plans succeeded, and he earned more praise because he worked for the Church and not for himself.

Julius kept the Orsini and Colonna families quiet, because the Church was now too strong to challenge. They also had no cardinals of their own, and cardinals, Machiavelli says, are the usual cause of trouble among the barons.
Machiavelli ends the chapter by praising Pope Leo X, who was a Medici and the uncle of the young Lorenzo. Others made the Church great by arms, he says, and Leo will make it great by goodness.
Machiavelli says every state rests on good laws and good arms, and that good laws cannot exist without good arms. He then turns to soldiers, and warns that hired soldiers are useless and dangerous.
Hired soldiers have no reason to stay in the field except a little pay, which is not enough to make them die for you. They are happy to serve in peace, but when war comes they run away or leave.

Italy's armies were mostly hired soldiers, and in 1494 King Charles VIII of France marched through the country almost unopposed. People joked that he took Italy with chalk, because his men only had to mark the houses where they would sleep.
A hired captain is either skilful or not, and either way he is a danger. If he is skilful he will want power for himself, and if he is not he will lose your battles.
A prince should lead his army in person, and a republic should send its own citizens to command it. Rome and Sparta stayed armed and free for many centuries, and the Swiss are armed and free today.
After its first war with Rome, Carthage was nearly crushed by its own hired soldiers. Thebes gave command of its army to Philip of Macedon, and he later took away the city's freedom.

When Duke Filippo of Milan died, the Milanese hired Francesco Sforza to fight the Venetians. After he beat the Venetians at Caravaggio, he joined them against the Milanese and later made himself duke.
Venice grew great with its own sailors, but on land it began to hire captains. In 1509, at the battle of Vailà, it lost in one day much of what it had taken centuries to win.
Florence also used hired captains, and it was lucky that none of them won too much. If the English captain John Hawkwood or Paolo Vitelli had succeeded, Florence would have been at their mercy.
Auxiliary soldiers are troops that a stronger ruler lends to help you. If they lose, you are ruined, and if they win, you become their prisoner.

Florence once borrowed ten thousand French soldiers to take Pisa and was in more danger than ever. The Emperor of Constantinople brought in ten thousand Turks to fight his neighbours, and they never left.

Machiavelli says that borrowed troops are even more dangerous than hired ones, because they are united and obey someone else. Hired soldiers are slower to turn on you, because they are not one body and their leader needs time and a good chance.
Borgia first used French soldiers, then hired Orsini soldiers, and finally his own men. His reputation grew each time, and it was highest when everyone saw that he commanded his own army.
Hiero of Syracuse soon saw that his hired soldiers were useless. He could neither keep them nor send them away, so he had them all killed and fought with his own men.
When David offered to fight Goliath, King Saul gave him his own armour. David took it off, because he could not use it well, and chose to fight with his sling.

Charles VII of France built an army of his own, but his son Louis XI dropped the foot soldiers and hired Swiss troops. Machiavelli says this weakened France, because a state without its own arms is never secure.

Chapter fourteen says that a prince should think of nothing but war and its training. Francesco Sforza rose to be Duke of Milan because he was armed, but his sons lost it by avoiding the hardships of war.

In peace a prince should keep his body hard by hunting, and study how hills, valleys, rivers and marshes lie. This teaches him to defend his own country, and it helps him to understand any other country quickly.
