Philopoemen, a leader of the Achaeans, thought about war even in peace. On walks with his friends he would stop and ask what an army should do if an enemy stood on a nearby hill.
To train his mind, a prince should read history and study why great leaders won or lost. He should also pick a hero to imitate, as Alexander followed Achilles and Caesar followed Alexander.

Chapter fifteen begins with a warning that Machiavelli will depart from other writers. He wants to write what is useful, so he will deal with the truth of things as they are and not with imagined republics.
Machiavelli says that how people live is very different from how they ought to live. A man who wants to be good in everything will be ruined among so many who are not good.

Everyone would praise a prince who had all the good qualities, Machiavelli admits, but human life does not allow it. So the prince must be wise enough to avoid the faults that would cost him his state.
Machiavelli adds a surprising warning about how things look and what they lead to. A quality that seems like virtue may destroy a prince, while one that seems like vice may protect him.

It is good to be thought generous, Machiavelli says, but a prince who wants that name must spend on show after show. In the end he will run out of money and have to tax his people heavily, which makes him hated.
A generous prince who has to stop giving will suddenly be called a miser. A careful prince can accept that name, Machiavelli says, because his savings let him defend the state without new taxes.

Machiavelli says that in his own time only rulers thought miserly did great things. Julius II won the papacy by generosity but then saved money for war, and Louis XII of France fought many wars without extra taxes.
Some people say Caesar rose to power by being generous. Machiavelli replies that generosity helps a man on his way up, but harms him once he rules, as it would have harmed Caesar.

A prince who leads armies and lives on plunder and ransoms must give freely, or his soldiers will not follow him. He can do this safely, because spending what belongs to others adds to his reputation, as it did for Cyrus, Caesar and Alexander.
Machiavelli says nothing wastes itself like generosity, because while you use it you lose the means to use it. A prince who gives too much becomes either poor and despised, or greedy and hated.

Every prince wants to be thought merciful, Machiavelli says, but he must not use mercy badly. Cesare Borgia was called cruel, yet he brought peace to the Romagna, while Florence let Pistoia fall into ruin to avoid seeming harsh.

A few harsh punishments, Machiavelli says, can be kinder than too much mercy. Mercy that lets disorder grow causes killing and robbery that harms everyone, while a ruler's punishment harms only one person.
Machiavelli adds that a prince must be slow to believe and slow to act. He should act with prudence and humanity, so that he is neither careless through trust nor unbearable through suspicion.
Machiavelli asks whether it is better for a prince to be loved or to be feared. A prince would like to be both, he answers, but since that is hard, it is safer to be feared if he must choose.

Machiavelli says that people in general are ungrateful, changeable, deceitful, cowardly and greedy. While you help them, they promise you their lives and their children, but when real danger comes close, they turn away.

Friendships that are bought with money are not really owned, and they cannot be spent when the need comes. Love is a chain of duty that people break when it suits them, while fear is a dread of punishment that never leaves.

A prince should be feared without being hated, Machiavelli says, by keeping away from his subjects' property and their wives and daughters. People forget the death of a father sooner, he says, than the loss of an inheritance.

A general with a big army must not mind being called cruel, Machiavelli says, or he cannot keep it united. Hannibal led soldiers of many nations in foreign lands, and they never quarrelled with each other or with him.
Machiavelli gives the opposite case in Scipio, a great Roman general whose army rebelled in Spain. He says this came from Scipio's mercy, which gave the soldiers more freedom than discipline allows.
Machiavelli concludes that people love at their own will but fear at the prince's will. A wise prince therefore builds on what he controls himself, and above all he avoids being hated.

Everyone agrees that it is praiseworthy for a prince to keep his word. Yet Machiavelli says that the princes who did great things in his time often cared little for promises and knew how to outwit others.

Machiavelli says there are two ways to fight, with laws, as men do, and with force, as beasts do. In the old stories the centaur Chiron, half man and half beast, taught Achilles, to show that a prince must know both.
Among the beasts, Machiavelli says, a prince should choose the fox and the lion. The lion cannot see traps and the fox cannot scare wolves, so a prince must be both.

Machiavelli says that a prudent ruler need not keep a promise when it hurts him and the reasons for it have gone. If all men were good, this advice would be wrong, but they are not, and they will not keep faith with him.
But the fox must hide his nature well, Machiavelli says, and be a great pretender. People are so simple and so busy with present needs that a deceiver will always find someone ready to be deceived.

Machiavelli gives a recent example, Pope Alexander VI, who thought about nothing but deceiving people. He swore the strongest oaths and kept them least, yet his tricks always worked, because he knew how people are.
A prince need not have every good quality, Machiavelli says, but he must seem to have them. He should be good when he can, but he must also know how to do wrong when necessity demands it.
A prince must take great care that every word from his mouth sounds merciful, faithful, honest, humane and religious. Of these five, Machiavelli says, appearing religious is the most necessary.

People judge more with their eyes than with their hands, Machiavelli says: everyone sees what you seem, but few know what you are. In the actions of princes, where nobody can appeal to a judge, people look only at the result.
Machiavelli ends the chapter with a sly example of a prince of his own day, whom he says it is not good to name. This ruler preaches only peace and faith, yet he is a great enemy of both.
Chapter nineteen says that a prince should avoid being hated or despised. He is hated if he takes people's property, and despised if he seems changeable, weak or unable to make up his mind.
A prince with a strong reputation is hard to plot against and hard to attack. He has two fears, his own subjects and foreign powers, and he guards against the second with good arms and good friends.

One of the best defences against plots, Machiavelli says, is not to be hated by the people. A plotter needs helpers, any of whom might betray him, while the prince has the law, his friends and his people.

In 1445 the Canneschi family killed Annibale Bentivoglio, the ruler of Bologna, and left only a baby son. The people rose at once against the plotters, and then fetched another Bentivoglio from Florence to rule until the child grew up.

In France, Machiavelli says, the Parlement acts as a third judge between the king, the nobles and the people. This protects the king, because others take the blame for unpopular decisions, while he keeps the favours for himself.

Some readers think the Roman emperors disprove his advice, because several good emperors were killed. Machiavelli answers that the emperors had a third difficulty, the greed and cruelty of their own soldiers.

Marcus Aurelius lived and died honoured, because he inherited the empire and kept soldiers and people in their places. Pertinax tried to make the soldiers live honestly and they killed him within months, and Alexander Severus was despised for obeying his mother.
Septimius Severus used the cunning of a fox and the strength of a lion. He marched on Rome to avenge Pertinax and became emperor, then defeated one rival and tricked the other.

Caracalla was a fine soldier, but his terrible cruelty made everyone hate him, and a centurion killed him. Commodus fought as a gladiator and lost the soldiers' respect, and Maximinus was hated for his cruelty and despised for his low birth.

In modern states, Machiavelli says, it is more important to please the people than the soldiers, except in Turkey and Egypt. A new prince should take from Severus what he needs to found his state, and from Marcus what he needs to keep it.

Some princes disarmed their subjects to hold their states, but Machiavelli says a new prince should do the opposite. When he arms his people, their weapons become his, and those he doubted become loyal.

Wise rulers once said that Pistoia should be held by factions and Pisa by fortresses. Machiavelli disagrees, because a divided city is lost at once when an enemy comes, as the Venetians found after Vailà.

Machiavelli says that princes grow great by overcoming the difficulties that enemies put in their way. He also notes that men who were once suspected, like those who served Pandolfo Petrucci of Siena, often prove more loyal than early friends.

Princes have often built fortresses to hold their states, but others have torn them down. Machiavelli says their value depends on the times, and the castle Francesco Sforza built in Milan brought his family endless trouble.
The best fortress, Machiavelli says, is not to be hated by the people. The Countess of Forlì was saved by her fortress once, but not when Cesare Borgia attacked and her people sided with him.
Machiavelli says nothing makes a prince respected like great undertakings. Ferdinand of Aragon began his reign with a war against Granada, which kept his nobles too busy for plots.

Ferdinand went on from Granada to wars in Africa, Italy and France, so his subjects were always watching and never plotting. He also drove many Jews out of Spain under the cover of religion, an act that Machiavelli calls a pious cruelty.
A prince is also respected when he openly takes sides, Machiavelli says. If two powers fight and he stays neutral, he will be the prey of the winner, and the loser will not help him either.

If the prince joins the winner, the winner owes him something, and if he joins the loser, he will at least be sheltered. But he should never ally with a stronger prince to attack others unless he must, for a winning ally makes him a prisoner.
A prince should honour talent and let his citizens farm and trade without fear of seizure or heavy taxes. He should reward those who improve the state and sometimes give festivals for the people.

The first sign of a ruler's brains, Machiavelli says, is the men he has around him. If they are capable and faithful, people think him wise, as they did Pandolfo Petrucci of Siena, who employed Antonio da Venafro.

Machiavelli describes three kinds of brain, one that understands by itself, one that can judge what others show it, and one that does neither. The third kind is useless, and a prince who is not the first must at least be the second.

A minister who thinks more of himself than of the prince can never be trusted, Machiavelli says. The prince should keep a good minister loyal by honouring and rewarding him, so that he sees he cannot stand without the prince.

Courts are full of flatterers, Machiavelli says, and princes find it hard to resist them because everyone likes to hear good things about himself. The only defence is to let people know that truth will not offend you, yet if everyone may speak freely, he loses respect.
A wise prince picks a few wise men and lets only them tell him the truth, about things he asks. He then decides for himself and sticks to his decision.

Emperor Maximilian told no one his plans, but when people heard them they argued, and he changed his mind. Machiavelli says a prince should take advice only when he asks for it, and good advice must come from his own good sense.

Chapter twenty-four says that a new prince who follows this advice will soon seem like an old ruler. People look closely at a new prince, and when his actions are good, they enjoy the present and seek nothing else.

Machiavelli looks at the Italian lords of his time who lost their states, such as the King of Naples and the Duke of Milan. He finds the same faults in each, weak arms, and either a hostile people or nobles they could not control.

Philip of Macedon, the king beaten by Titus Quintius, had little power compared with Rome and Greece. But he was a soldier who kept his people content and his nobles secure, so he fought for years and still kept his kingdom.

Machiavelli says the fallen princes of Italy should blame their own laziness, not Fortune. In quiet times they never imagined a storm, and when it came they ran away and hoped that the people would call them back.

Chapter twenty-five begins with a common belief that fortune and God govern the world, so that human wisdom can do nothing. Machiavelli admits that, thinking about the great changes of his own time, he has sometimes leaned that way himself.
Machiavelli does not want to deny that people have free will. So he suggests that fortune decides about half of our actions and leaves the other half to us.
Machiavelli compares fortune to a violent river that floods the plains and tears down trees and buildings. Everyone runs away from it, and nobody can stop it while it rages.
Even so, people could build dikes in quiet times, Machiavelli says, so that a flood runs in a channel or does less harm. Fortune shows her power where no one has prepared to resist her.

Italy, Machiavelli says, is a country without dikes or banks, where the great floods of change have done the most damage. If it had been defended with enough courage, like Germany, Spain and France, the flood would have done far less harm.

One sees a prince happy today and ruined tomorrow, Machiavelli says, without any change in his character. He believes that a prince succeeds when his way of acting fits the times, and fails when it does not.

Men chase glory and riches in different ways, Machiavelli says: some are careful and some are bold. Two careful men may have different results, while a careful man and a bold man may both succeed, because of the times.

A careful ruler does well while times suit caution, but he is ruined when they change, because he cannot change his own nature. Even a very wise man, Machiavelli says, seldom leaves the road that has always brought him success.
Pope Julius II acted boldly in everything, and the times suited him. In 1506 he marched on Bologna in person, before anyone was ready, and Spain and Venice froze while France followed him.

Julius died before the times changed, so his boldness was never tested. Machiavelli concludes that boldness is better than caution, and he ends with a famous image of Fortune as a woman who favours the young.
In the last chapter Machiavelli asks whether the time is right in Italy for a new prince to help the people. He decides that so many things point the same way that he knows no better moment.
Machiavelli says that, like Israel in Egypt, Italy had been brought as low as it could go. She was more enslaved than the Hebrews, more scattered than the Athenians, and she had no head and no order.

A spark of hope had shown in one man, but fortune turned against him, and Italy now waits for someone to heal her wounds. Machiavelli says that she would follow any banner raised for her, and that the Medici house is the best hope she has.
Machiavelli says the great founders were only men, and this cause is as just as theirs. He quotes Livy that a war is just when it is necessary, and adds that God will not do everything for us.

Machiavelli says that Italians are superior in strength and skill in duels and small fights, but they do badly in armies. The cause, he says, is weak leaders, because those who know are not obeyed and everyone thinks he knows.

Before anything else, Machiavelli says, the Medici must raise an army of their own people, because there are no better soldiers. Swiss and Spanish infantry are feared, but each has a weakness that a new kind of army could use.

Machiavelli imagines the love and tears with which a liberator would be welcomed in every province. He ends the book with lines by Petrarch saying that courage will take up arms against fury and the fight will be short.
The Medici did not give Machiavelli the post that he hoped for, and the call to free Italy was never answered. Lorenzo, the young man to whom the book was dedicated, died in 1519 at only twenty-six.
In these years Machiavelli wrote the Discourses on Livy, which praise the Roman republic, and a comedy called Mandragola. He also wrote The Art of War, which was printed in 1521, in his own lifetime.
In 1520 Cardinal Giulio de' Medici asked Machiavelli to write a history of Florence. When Giulio became Pope Clement VII, Machiavelli presented the finished work to him in 1526.
In 1527 the Medici were driven out and the republic returned, but the new rulers did not trust him. Machiavelli died that June, aged fifty-eight, and he lies in Santa Croce in Florence.
The Prince was not printed while Machiavelli lived, and it passed from hand to hand in copies written by hand. It was first printed in 1532 in Rome and Florence, five years after his death.
An English cardinal, Reginald Pole, said The Prince seemed to have been written by the hand of Satan. In 1559 the Catholic Church put all of Machiavelli's works on its list of banned books.

In the England of Queen Elizabeth, stage villains who plotted in secret were called Machiavels. Marlowe opened one play with a speech by Machiavel himself, and Shakespeare wrote of a murderous Machiavel.

In 1740 Frederick of Prussia published a book, edited by Voltaire, that attacked Machiavelli and said that rulers should be honest and just. Within months, as king, he marched his army into Silesia without warning.

In 1762 the French thinker Rousseau wrote that Machiavelli pretended to teach kings but really taught the people. In the 1800s Italian patriots read his last chapter as a call to unite their country, which became one state in 1861.

Two words matter most in the book: virtù, which means skill, energy and courage rather than goodness, and fortuna, which means luck and circumstance. The famous saying that the end justifies the means does not appear in it, although chapter eighteen says that one looks to the end.
Some scholars say The Prince is honest advice from an experienced official. Others say it is a warning to ordinary people, a secret satire, or simply a clever job application to the Medici.

Modern readers still find useful ideas in The Prince: plan ahead, choose honest advisers, avoid flatterers and build your own strength. But it was written for a ruler in 1513, so its advice on cruelty and deceit belongs to history, not to daily life.
The Prince is short, sharp and still argued about. Read it, compare it with other views, and decide for yourself how far a good aim can excuse hard means.
C1C2: In the summer of 1498, when he was twenty-nine, Machiavelli was chosen as a senior secretary of the republic of Florence, a post that soon carried him into the middle of its dealings with other states. He was neither a nobleman nor a rich man, and he owed the job to a quick mind, a clear style and a gift for seeing how power really works. For the next fourteen years he served the city faithfully, and nearly everything he later wrote grew out of what he learned there.

His work sent him on many missions, to the French court of Louis XII, to Pope Julius II and to the German emperor Maximilian. On the road he wrote long, sharp reports in which he looked less at what rulers said than at what they did and why they did it. Years of such watching taught him how kings, popes and generals really behave when much is at stake.

At the end of 1502 the republic sent Machiavelli to the court of Cesare Borgia, a young soldier and the son of a pope, who was carving a new state out of central Italy. For some three months he followed Borgia's camp, studying his speed, his secrecy and his readiness to strike without warning. He admired some of what he saw, and years later he remembered it when he came to write about princes.

Machiavelli had long believed that hired soldiers were slow, greedy and unreliable, and that a free city ought to defend itself with its own men. In 1506 he persuaded the government to raise a militia of country people, and he travelled from village to village to enrol and train them. Three years later this militia helped to bring the rebel city of Pisa back under Florence, and it was the proudest work of his career.

In August 1512 a Spanish army, sent to bring back the Medici, stormed the small town of Prato, and the untrained militia that Machiavelli had raised broke and ran. The shock was enough to topple the republic, for its leader, Piero Soderini, left the city within days and the Medici returned after eighteen years in exile. For Machiavelli it was a bitter lesson, because the first great test of his citizen army had ended in a rout.

In November 1512 the Medici dismissed Machiavelli from every post he held, and ordered him to stay within the lands of Florence and to keep out of the government palace. At forty-three he was suddenly a man without an income, a career or a voice in the affairs he understood best. He had a wife and several young children, and very little money to feed them.

In February 1513 the police found his name on a list kept by young men who were plotting against the Medici, and Machiavelli was arrested. He was questioned under torture, hauled up by his wrists on a rope, yet he insisted that he knew nothing of any plot. A few weeks later the election of a Medici pope, Leo X, brought a general pardon, and he walked out of prison with his life and his freedom but not his career.

Shut out from the centre of power, Machiavelli went to live with his family on a small farm at Sant'Andrea, in the hills some miles south of Florence. The house was plain and the land was poor, and he spent his days among woodcutters, tenants and farm animals. For a man who had talked with kings and popes, the silence was hard to bear.

Each morning he went out to watch the cutting of his wood and to read a little poetry beside a spring, and then he walked to the inn on the road to chat with travellers. After dinner he returned to play cards and backgammon with the innkeeper, a butcher, a miller and two kiln workers, and their quarrels over a penny could be heard in the next village. He wrote afterwards that he let himself sink into this low company only to wipe the mould from his brain, and to see whether Fortune would be ashamed of treating him so.

At nightfall he left the mud of the farm at the door, put on the fine robes of the court and entered the study where his old books waited. There, he told his friend Francesco Vettori, he talked with the great men of antiquity, who welcomed him kindly and answered every question he put to them. Out of those evenings, in 1513, came a little work on principalities, which he called On Principalities and which the world now knows as The Prince.

Machiavelli addressed his little book to Lorenzo de' Medici, a young member of the family that now governed Florence, and he did so with a very practical hope. He was poor and out of work, and he wanted the new rulers to see that a man of his experience could still be of use. The dedication is polite, careful and a little anxious, as one would expect from a man who longed to be employed.

People who wish to win a prince's favour, Machiavelli remarks, usually bring him horses, weapons, cloth of gold or jewels, but he has none of these things to offer. What he does possess is his knowledge of the actions of great men, gained through long experience of present affairs and a ceaseless study of the past. He has gathered it into a small book, and he asks the young lord to accept it.

He explains why a man of humble rank dares to write about kings, using a picture from art. Those who draw landscapes, he says, stand in the plain to see the mountains and on a hill to see the valleys, so one must be a prince to know the people and one of the people to know princes. His own low rank, he suggests, is therefore a kind of qualification for the task.

He closes with a polite request, wrapped in flattery and humility, that the young lord should take notice of him. If Lorenzo will only turn his eyes, now and then, from the heights where he stands to the low places where the author lives, he will see how undeservedly Machiavelli has suffered. It is a plea for a job, dressed in the language of courtesy and offered by a man with nothing left to lose.

The book opens with a very short chapter that sorts every state that has ever held power over people into two kinds, republics and principalities. A principality is a state ruled by a single man, and Machiavelli says plainly that he will leave republics to another place and speak here only of princes. He will explain how principalities are won, how they are held and why they are lost.

Machiavelli says that principalities are either hereditary, handed down within one family, or new. Some new ones are made from nothing, as Milan was by Francesco Sforza, while others are added like limbs to the old state of a prince who has conquered them, as Naples was to the King of Spain. A state may be won by the prince's own arms or by the arms of others, and by good fortune or by his own ability.

Of all kinds of state, Machiavelli says, the hereditary one is the easiest to keep, because the people are used to the ruling family and have grown comfortable with its ways. The prince has only to avoid breaking old customs and to deal sensibly with each new difficulty as it appears. Even a prince of modest ability, he adds, will hold his place unless some unusual and excessive force removes him.

Machiavelli gives a recent example, the Duke of Ferrara, whose small state stood firm against the Venetians in 1484 and against Pope Julius II in 1510. The duke's strength lay less in his army than in the age of his family's rule, for his people had never known another lord. A stranger in his place, Machiavelli implies, would have fallen at the first blow.

The natural prince, Machiavelli observes, has fewer reasons and less need to give offence, and so it is only to be expected that he will be better loved by his people. Unless some unusual vice makes him hated, they will probably feel a natural goodwill towards the family that has always ruled them. In the length and steadiness of his rule the memory of earlier upheavals fades away.

Machiavelli ends the chapter with a vivid image taken from the work of builders. Just as a mason leaves rough stones sticking out of a wall so that the next section can be fitted to it, he says, one change in a state always leaves a toothing for another. A long and steady rule therefore wipes out both the memory and the causes of upheaval.

Chapter three turns to mixed principalities, in which a new territory is added to a prince's old lands, and here the trouble begins. Men change their masters gladly, Machiavelli says, because they believe they will fare better, and this hope leads them to take up arms against the old ruler. Experience soon shows them that they have made things worse, because the new lord is usually harder on them than the old one was.

A conqueror, Machiavelli explains, must nearly always offend the people of the new land, by quartering soldiers on them and by the countless other injuries that follow a conquest. He makes enemies of everyone he has hurt, and he cannot keep as friends those who helped him to power, because he can never reward them as richly as they expected. However strong his army may be, he still needs the goodwill of the local people to enter a province at all.

When a province that has rebelled is conquered again, Machiavelli says, it is lost less easily, because the ruler can use the revolt as an excuse to punish the guilty, expose the doubtful and strengthen the weakest places. He points to Louis XII and Milan: the first time, it was enough for Duke Ludovico to make a little noise at the borders to drive the French out. The second time, the whole world had to turn against the French king, and his armies had to be destroyed or chased out of Italy.

If the conquered territory lies in the same region and shares the language of the old one, Machiavelli says, it is easy to hold, above all if its people are unaccustomed to liberty. It is enough to extinguish the dynasty of the former prince and then to leave the old laws and taxes undisturbed, so that men can go on living peacefully as before. France has kept Burgundy, Brittany, Gascony and Normandy for generations in just this way, and their slight differences of dialect have done little harm.

The real difficulties begin, Machiavelli says, when a land differs from the conqueror's own in language, customs and laws, for then he needs great luck and great effort to keep it. One of the best remedies is for the conqueror to go and live there himself, as the Turk did in Greece, because on the spot he sees trouble as it starts and can cure it at once. Far away, he hears of disorder only when it is already too big to mend.

The second remedy, Machiavelli says, is to plant colonies of settlers in one or two key places, where they will hold the new land as shackles hold a prisoner. They cost the prince almost nothing and injure only the few families whose fields and houses are given to the settlers, who are poor, scattered and unable to take revenge. An army of occupation would cost far more, for it would swallow the revenues of the land and trouble every household in it.

A ruler of such a land, Machiavelli advises, should make himself the leader and protector of the weaker neighbouring states and find ways to weaken the strong ones. He must be careful never to let a foreigner as powerful as himself enter the country, because discontented men will always call in a stranger, whether from ambition or from fear. The Aetolians, he notes, did exactly this when they brought the Romans into Greece.

The Romans, Machiavelli says, always saw troubles from afar and cured them while they were small, and they never let a disorder run on in order to avoid a war. They knew that a war is not avoided but only put off, to the advantage of others, and so they chose to fight Philip and Antiochus in Greece rather than meet them later in Italy. They had no faith in the saying of the wise men of his day, that one should enjoy the benefit of time, and trusted instead in their own courage and foresight.

Machiavelli explains the need for foresight with an image borrowed from the doctors of his day. Of a wasting fever, they say, at the beginning it is easy to cure and hard to recognise, but in time, if it has been neither noticed nor treated, it becomes easy to recognise and hard to cure. The same happens in states: only a prudent ruler sees evils while they are far off, and when they have grown so large that everyone sees them, no remedy is left.

Louis XII of France, Machiavelli says, made five mistakes in Italy: he destroyed the weaker powers, made a strong one stronger, brought in a mighty foreigner, did not go to live there and sent no colonies. Even so, he might have survived them all had he not added a sixth by taking land from the Venetians. When the Cardinal of Rouen told Machiavelli that Italians knew nothing about war, Machiavelli answered that the French knew nothing about government, or they would never have let the Church grow so great.

Chapter four begins with a puzzle: Alexander the Great made himself master of Asia in a few short years and died soon after, so one might expect his new empire to have fallen apart. Yet the lands he had won from King Darius did not rebel against his successors, who suffered no trouble except what grew out of their own ambitions. Machiavelli sets out to explain why, and his answer depends on how a state is governed.

Every principality known to him, Machiavelli says, is governed in one of two ways: by a prince who rules through servants, or by a prince who rules among barons. In the empire of the Turk the servants serve only by his favour, whereas in France the barons hold their rank through ancient blood and have their own lands and subjects. This difference decides how hard such a state is to conquer and how hard it is to keep.

A state ruled like Turkey's is very hard to enter, Machiavelli says, because no great man in it can be tempted to call in the invader, and the prince's servants, who owe him everything, are not easily bribed. An attacker must therefore expect to find the enemy united, and must trust in his own strength rather than in the enemy's disorder. But once the ruler has been beaten in the field and cannot raise new armies, nothing remains to fear except his family, and when that is gone there is no one else the people will follow.

In a kingdom like France, Machiavelli says, a conqueror can find a way in by winning over one of the barons, for there are always discontented men who long for change. The same men who opened the gate will cause endless trouble afterwards, since he can neither satisfy them nor get rid of them, and it is not enough to end the old royal family. Every baron remains the head of a fresh rebellion, and whenever the chance comes the conqueror will lose the state.

Because Darius had governed like the Turk, Machiavelli says, Alexander had only to defeat him in the field and the empire was his, and his successors kept it in peace. The Romans met a different fate in Spain, Gaul and Greece, where so many small states had their own princes that revolts broke out again and again. Only when the memory of those old rulers faded, after generations of Roman power, did the provinces settle into obedience.

Chapter five asks how to hold a city that has been used to living under its own laws and in freedom, and Machiavelli names three ways. The conqueror can destroy it, he can go and live there himself, or he can let it keep its laws, take a tribute from it and set up a government of a few friends who will keep it loyal. The third way sounds the gentlest, since such a small government knows it cannot last without the prince's support, yet history shows that it does not always work.

Machiavelli recalls that the Spartans held Athens and Thebes by setting up in each a government of a few leading citizens, who were meant to be their friends and servants. In spite of this careful arrangement, both cities were lost to them, for the people remembered their freedom and hated the rulers they had been given. The experiment shows how little a clever plan can do against a people's longing to be free.

To keep Capua, Carthage and Numantia, Machiavelli says, the Romans destroyed them, and they never lost them. In Greece they tried a gentler way, leaving the cities free and letting them keep their laws, but it did not work, and in the end they had to destroy many of those cities in order to hold the province. He concludes grimly that there is no sure way to hold a free city except to ruin it.

Whoever takes a city used to freedom and does not destroy it, Machiavelli warns, can expect to be destroyed by it, for in every revolt it falls back on the name of liberty and its ancient customs. He knew this from his own experience as a Florentine, because Pisa, which had been under Florence for nearly a hundred years, threw off its yoke the moment the French king crossed the Alps. Neither time nor kindness will make such people forget, unless they are scattered far and wide.

Cities used to a prince are different, because when the old family dies out the people have no master to obey. Since they cannot agree on one of their own, they are slow to rise and easy to win. In republics, by contrast, there is more life, more hatred and a stronger wish for revenge, and the surest course there is either to destroy the city or to go and live among its people.

Chapter six deals with new principalities won by a man's own arms and ability, and it begins with advice about whom to imitate. Most people, Machiavelli says, walk along roads already beaten by others, and since nobody can fully match the greatness of a hero, a wise man should follow the paths of the best. He should behave like a clever archer, who, seeing that his mark is far away, aims much higher than the target so that the height of his aim will carry the arrow to it.

The great founders, Machiavelli says, owed nothing to fortune except the opportunity, which gave them the material on which to impose the shape they wanted. Moses needed the people of Israel to be oppressed in Egypt, so that they would gladly follow him out of bondage, and Cyrus needed the Persians to be discontented with the Medes, who had grown soft through long peace. Without such openings their talents would have been wasted, and without their talents the openings would have come in vain.

Romulus, by the old story, was cast out of Alba as a baby, and so he became in time the king and founder of Rome. Theseus found the Athenians scattered and brought them together in one city, where they could live under his laws. In each case, Machiavelli says, opportunity made the man fortunate and his ability made the opportunity count, so that their countries were honoured and became very prosperous.

There is nothing harder to handle, Machiavelli declares, nor more doubtful in its outcome, nor more dangerous to manage, than to take the lead in introducing a new order of things. The innovator makes enemies of everyone who prospers under the old order, and he has only lukewarm defenders among those who might prosper under the new. This coolness comes partly from fear of opponents who have the law on their side, and partly from the human habit of doubting new things until they have been proved by experience.

Anyone who tries to introduce a new order, Machiavelli says, must first ask whether he stands on his own strength or depends on the help of others, that is, whether he must plead for support or can compel it. If he must plead, he always comes to a bad end and achieves nothing, because his supporters can walk away. If he can use force, however, he is rarely in danger, since he does not need anyone's belief to carry out his plans.

This is why, in his view, all the armed prophets won and all the unarmed ones came to ruin. The mood of a people is changeable, and it is easy to persuade them of something but hard to keep them persuaded, so a founder must be ready to make them believe by force when they believe no longer. Without arms, Moses, Cyrus, Theseus and Romulus could not have made their laws respected for long.

Machiavelli's own city supplied the best example in Fra Girolamo Savonarola, a preacher who led Florence for some years after 1494 and was ruined when the crowd began to doubt him. He had no means of holding those who still believed or of winning back those who did not, and he was hanged and burned in 1498. Machiavelli, then a young man in the city, followed these events closely and drew the lesson that a prophet without arms comes to grief.

To these great examples Machiavelli adds a smaller one, Hiero of Syracuse, who rose from private life to rule his city and was so able, a writer said, that he lacked nothing to reign except a kingdom. Fortune gave him nothing but the opportunity, for the Syracusans, hard pressed by their enemies, chose him as their captain and later as their prince. He replaced the old army and the old friends with new ones of his own, and so he laboured long to win power and little to keep it.

Chapter seven is about men who become princes through luck or through the arms of others. They rise with little effort, because they seem to fly, but their troubles all begin the moment they arrive, for they depend wholly on the will and fortune of whoever gave them the state, and both are inconstant. They do not know how to command, having lived as private men, and they cannot command either, since they have no loyal forces of their own.

To show how fragile such power is, Machiavelli sets two men from his own age side by side. Francesco Sforza, by his own talent, rose from private life to be Duke of Milan, and what he won with a thousand labours he kept with little trouble. Cesare Borgia, whom the people called Duke Valentino, gained his state through the fortune of his father and lost it with that fortune, although he did everything a wise and able man could do to put down roots.

Pope Alexander VI wished to make his son Cesare a great prince, and Machiavelli lists the difficulties that stood in his way. He could find no state to give him except lands of the Church, and if he took those, he knew that the Duke of Milan and the Venetians would object, since Faenza and Rimini were already under Venetian protection. Worse, the armies of Italy lay in the hands of men, chiefly the Orsini and Colonna families, who had every reason to fear a pope grown too strong.

The pope saw that the old order of Italy had to be thrown into confusion, and he found the Venetians already willing to bring the French back into the country. Far from opposing them, he made the French king's return easier by dissolving Louis XII's old marriage, a favour for which Louis was glad to repay him. French soldiers then marched into Italy, and with their help Cesare Borgia set out to conquer the cities of the Romagna.

With a French army beside him, Duke Valentino took the Romagna, and he wished to hold it and go further. Two things held him back, for he doubted the loyalty of the Orsini soldiers whom he had been using, and he feared that the king of France might not allow him to go on. He suspected that the Orsini might not only hinder his conquests but take them from him.

In 1502 the Orsini and other captains, who had joined in a conspiracy against the duke, were persuaded by his friendly letters and gifts to make peace with him. He then invited them to meet him at Senigallia, and on the last day of the year he had them seized, and two of them, Vitellozzo Vitelli and Oliverotto da Fermo, were put to death that night. Machiavelli was with the duke's court in those weeks and wrote a famous account of the affair, in which he admires its cleverness without hiding its cruelty.

Machiavelli says that the Romagna had long been ruled by weak lords, who robbed their subjects rather than correcting them, so that the whole province was full of theft, quarrels and every kind of violence. Borgia judged that it needed firm government before it could be peaceful and obedient, and he sent Remirro de Orco, a cruel and efficient man, with complete power. In a short time Remirro had brought the region to peace and unity, and he had won a great reputation for it.

Borgia soon judged that such great power was no longer needed, and since he feared that it would breed hatred, he set up a civil court with an excellent president. To wash away the hatred already felt, he wished to show that the harshness had come from his minister and not from himself. So one morning he had Remirro put to death and left in the square at Cesena, with a block of wood and a bloody knife beside him, and the sight left the people at once satisfied and stunned.

Borgia knew that his power rested on his father's life, so he made careful plans for the day when the pope would die. He meant to destroy the families of the lords he had robbed, to win the nobles of Rome, to control the College of Cardinals and to conquer enough land to resist a first attack. By the time Alexander died he had achieved the first three and nearly the fourth, and Machiavelli notes that Florence, his own city, would soon have had no remedy against him.

In August 1503 the pope died, and the duke, who was himself gravely ill, found his new state still unfinished, with two powerful enemy armies close by. Even so, Machiavelli says, his foundations were so well laid that the Romagna waited for him for more than a month, and in Rome, though half dead, he stayed safe. He had such courage and understood so well how men are won or lost that, with his health and without those armies, he would have overcome every difficulty.

When a new pope had to be chosen, the duke could at least have prevented the election of any cardinal whom he had offended or who had reason to fear him. Instead he supported Giuliano della Rovere, an old enemy, trusting that a new favour would wipe out an old injury. Anyone who believes that among great men new benefits make old injuries forgotten, Machiavelli declares, deceives himself, and this error was the cause of Borgia's final ruin.

Julius II soon turned against the duke, took the Romagna from him and later had him arrested, and in 1507, far from home, Borgia died in a small battle in Spain. Yet Machiavelli can find nothing in his conduct to reproach, except the choice of Julius, and he holds him up as the example for anyone who rises by fortune and the arms of others. A new prince who needs to win friends, to conquer by force or fraud, to be loved and feared and to build a new army, he says, will find no fresher model.

Chapter eight adds two more ways of becoming a prince that cannot be put down wholly to luck or to ability. A man may rise by some wicked and criminal path, or a private citizen may become the ruler of his own city through the favour of his fellow citizens. Machiavelli deals with the first now and saves the second for chapter nine, and he gives vivid examples from ancient and recent times.

Agathocles of Syracuse was the son of a potter and began from the lowest rung of society, and Machiavelli says that his life was wicked at every stage. Yet he joined his wickedness to such strength of body and spirit that, once he entered the army, he rose through its ranks until he became the praetor, or chief magistrate, of Syracuse. His career shows that a man of low birth can climb a very long way if he has talent and no scruples.

Having decided to rule by force, and having reached an understanding with Hamilcar, the Carthaginian general then fighting in Sicily, Agathocles summoned the senate and the people of Syracuse one morning as if to debate public business. At a signal his soldiers killed all the senators and the richest citizens, and with those men dead he seized the city and held it without any civil quarrel. It is a chilling story, and Machiavelli tells it without comment until he reaches its lesson.

Twice the Carthaginians defeated him, and in the end they besieged Syracuse itself, yet Agathocles not only defended his city but left part of his people to guard it and sailed with the rest to attack Africa. Within a short time he had freed Syracuse from the siege and brought Carthage to such extremity that it was forced to make an agreement with him. Under that agreement Carthage kept Africa while Agathocles kept Sicily, a result that nobody would have predicted from a potter's son.

Machiavelli admits that Agathocles was as bold and able in danger as the best of captains, and that his rise owed little to luck, since he fought his way up through the ranks of the army. Yet it cannot be called virtue, he says, to kill fellow citizens, betray friends and live without faith, pity or religion, because such methods may win a man power but never glory. His savage cruelty, together with endless wickedness, keeps him out of the company of the most admired men.

Oliverotto da Fermo, left an orphan as a boy, was brought up by his mother's brother, Giovanni Fogliani, and sent as a young man to learn the soldier's trade under the Vitelli. He was quick, strong and clever, and he soon rose to be the first man in the company of Vitellozzo Vitelli, but he felt it demeaning to serve under others. With the help of some citizens of Fermo who preferred the slavery of their city to its freedom, and with the backing of Vitellozzo, he made up his mind to seize Fermo.

Oliverotto wrote to his uncle that he wished to visit his home with a hundred horsemen, and after he was received with honour, he gave a grand banquet for Giovanni Fogliani and the first men of Fermo. In the middle of the feast he raised serious talk and withdrew to another room as if to discuss it in private, and when the guests followed, soldiers came out of hiding and killed them. Within a year he was master of Fermo and feared by his neighbours, but he was strangled at Senigallia along with Vitellozzo, the teacher of his virtue and his wickedness.

Machiavelli wonders how Agathocles and a few men like him could live long and secure in their homelands after countless betrayals and cruelties, when many other rulers could not keep their states even in peaceful times. He believes that the answer lies in whether cruelty is well used or badly used, and he adds a careful phrase, that it may be called well used, if it is lawful to speak well of evil. The phrase shows that he knows he is speaking of evil, and that his subject is what keeps a ruler safe, not what is admirable.

Cruelties are well used, Machiavelli says, when they are done all at a stroke out of the need to make oneself secure, and are then not repeated but turned as far as possible into benefits for the subjects. They are badly used when they are few at the start but grow in number as time passes instead of coming to an end. Those who follow the first course can hope, like Agathocles, to find some remedy with God and with men, while those who follow the second cannot possibly last.

A man who seizes a state, Machiavelli says, should decide at the start every injury he must inflict and carry them all out at a stroke, so that he need not repeat them daily and can then reassure his people. Injuries should be done together, so that being tasted less they give less offence, while benefits should be handed out little by little, so that they are tasted better. A ruler who waits until trouble comes will find that it is too late for harshness to help him and that favours are seen as forced and win him no thanks.

Chapter nine turns to the civil principality, in which a private citizen becomes prince of his own city, not through crime or intolerable violence but through the favour of his fellow citizens. To reach it, Machiavelli says, one needs neither wholly ability nor wholly fortune but rather a fortunate kind of cunning. He adds that a man climbs to this position either with the support of the people or with the support of the great.

In every city, Machiavelli observes, one finds two opposed humours, or moods: the people do not wish to be commanded or oppressed by the great, and the great desire to command and oppress the people. From this clash of appetites, he says, one of three results follows in each city, which is either a principality, or liberty, or licence. The prince who rises must therefore know which of the two sides has raised him, because it decides how he must rule.

A prince raised by the great, Machiavelli says, keeps his place with more difficulty, because he finds himself surrounded by many who think they are his equals and whom he can neither command nor manage as he wishes. The prince raised by the people, on the other hand, stands alone, and around him there are few or none who are not ready to obey. The nobles who make a prince, in short, expect to rule under his shadow, while the people merely want a defender.

The aims of the people are more honourable than those of the great, Machiavelli says, for the people only want not to be oppressed, while the great want to oppress. The worst a prince can expect from a hostile people is to be abandoned, whereas hostile nobles may also turn against him, and since they are wiser and craftier they always have time to join whoever seems likely to win. The prince must live with the same people for ever, but he can make and unmake nobles every day, taking away or giving them rank as he pleases.

Machiavelli says that the great should be judged by whether they tie their fortunes entirely to the prince. Those who do, and who are not greedy, deserve to be honoured and loved, and those who hold back from timidity or a lack of spirit can be used, especially if they give good advice. But those who hold back out of ambition are thinking more of themselves than of the prince, and he must fear them as open enemies, because in bad times they will always help to ruin him.

A prince, Machiavelli insists, must have the people friendly, or he has no remedy when adversity comes. Nabis, the ruler of Sparta, withstood all Greece and a victorious Roman army, and in danger he needed to deal only with a few suspects, which would not have sufficed if the people had been against him. The proverb that he who builds on the people builds on mud is true only of a private citizen who expects the crowd to rescue him, and not of a prince who can command and keeps his courage.

In chapter ten Machiavelli gives a simple test of a prince's strength: can he, with his own men and money, raise an army and meet any attacker in the field? If he can, he stands on his own feet, and if he cannot, and must shut himself behind walls and wait to be besieged, he depends on others and is weak. The second kind of prince can only be encouraged, he says, to fortify his town and to keep his people friendly.

The cities of Germany, Machiavelli says, are very free, hold little land around them and obey the emperor only when they please, for they fear neither him nor any neighbouring power. Each has proper ditches and walls and enough artillery, so that everyone thinks an attack on them would be a long and difficult business. They stand as a model of a state that has prepared for danger in good time.

In the public storehouses of these cities, Machiavelli says, there is always enough food, drink and fuel to last for a year. To keep the common people fed without loss to the public purse, the city also provides work for a year in the trades that are its strength and life, the trades by which the poor earn their living. It likewise honours military exercises, and has many regulations to keep its citizens in training.

A prince who has a strong city and is not hated cannot easily be attacked, Machiavelli says, because worldly things are so changeable that hardly anyone can keep an army idle in a siege for a whole year. If the enemy burns the countryside, it will be at the moment when men's minds are still hot for defence, and after a few days, when spirits have cooled, the damage is done and cannot be undone. The citizens then draw closer to the prince, since their houses have been burned in his defence, and men are bound as much by the favours they give as by those they receive.

Only the ecclesiastical principalities remain, Machiavelli says, and all their difficulties come before they are possessed, because they are won by ability or fortune but are kept without either. They are sustained by ancient religious customs, which are so strong and of such a kind that they keep their rulers in power however those rulers behave and live. It is a startling claim, and it sets the Church apart from every other state he has described.

Only these rulers, Machiavelli says, have states that they need not defend and subjects whom they need not govern, for the states are not taken from them and the subjects never think of leaving. Such principalities seem to him the only secure and happy ones, and he marvels at their good fortune. Since they are upheld by higher causes beyond the reach of the human mind, he declines to speak of them, for it would be the task of a presumptuous and foolish man to discuss what God raises and keeps.

Machiavelli asks how the Church grew so great in worldly power, since in his own lifetime a king of France came to tremble before it. Before King Charles VIII of France came into Italy in 1494, he explains, the country was shared among the pope, the Venetians, the King of Naples, the Duke of Milan and the Florentines. These five had two chief concerns, that no foreigner should enter Italy with an army and that none of them should grow too strong.

In Rome itself, Machiavelli says, the great families of the Orsini and Colonna, divided into two factions, were always quarrelling. Since they stood there with arms in their hands under the pope's very eyes, they kept the papacy weak and sickly, and even a courageous pope like Sixtus could not cure the trouble. The brevity of life was partly to blame, for a pope lived on average about ten years and could hardly put down one faction in that time.

Alexander VI, Machiavelli says, showed better than any pope in history how much could be won with money and armed force. His instrument was Duke Valentino, and his opportunity was the French invasion, and with them he did all the things described earlier in the story of the duke. Before him, the great Italian lords, down to the smallest baron, had thought little of the Church in worldly matters.

His intention, Machiavelli stresses, was never to make the Church great but to make the duke great, and yet what he did turned in the end to the Church's greatness. After the pope's death, with the duke destroyed, it was the Church that became heir to all his labours. Events had given a family scheme a very different result from the one its author had wished.

Julius II, who followed Alexander, found a Church that was already great, with the whole Romagna in its hands, the Roman barons broken and a way open to gather money in ways that had never been used before Alexander. He not only kept to these methods but extended them, and he took full advantage of the work that Alexander's blows had done. Machiavelli notes this in a plain tone, without praising the means by which the inheritance had been prepared.

Julius set himself three goals: to win Bologna, to break the power of the Venetians and to drive the French out of Italy. All these enterprises succeeded for him, Machiavelli says, and with the greater credit because he did everything to increase the Church and not to enrich any private person. Machiavelli's praise is warm, although the wars that Julius waged brought many sufferings to Italy.

Julius also kept the Orsini and Colonna factions where he found them, and two things held them down: the greatness of the Church, which frightened them, and the fact that they had no cardinals of their own. These factions, Machiavelli explains, are never quiet when they have cardinals, because cardinals foster parties which the barons are then forced to defend. The ambition of prelates is therefore the real source of the quarrels among the barons.

Machiavelli closes the chapter with a compliment that was clearly meant to be heard by the Medici family. Pope Leo X, he says, has found the papacy very powerful, and where others made it great with arms, he hopes that Leo, by his goodness and his endless other virtues, will make it greater and more venerable still. Since Leo was the uncle of the young man to whom the book is dedicated, the flattery is as practical as it is polite.

Chapter twelve begins with the foundations of every state, new or old, which are good laws and good arms, and since there can be no good laws without good arms, Machiavelli turns to arms. A prince's soldiers are his own, hired, borrowed from another power, or a mixture, and he says that hired and borrowed soldiers are both useless and dangerous. A ruler who relies on them will never be firm or secure, for such men are disunited, ambitious, undisciplined and unfaithful, bold among friends and cowardly before enemies.

The reason is simple, Machiavelli says: hired soldiers have no love and no motive to keep them in the field except a small wage, and that is not enough to make them willing to die for their master. They are eager to be his soldiers while he is not making war, but when war comes they either run away or go home. In peace, therefore, such a prince is robbed by his own men, and in war he is robbed by his enemies.

Italy's ruin, Machiavelli argues, was caused by nothing but its long reliance on hired soldiers, and the proof came in 1494, when King Charles VIII of France marched through the whole country with hardly a battle. People joked that he took Italy with chalk in his hand, since his men had only to mark the houses in which they would sleep. Some said that the sins of Italy had brought this about, but he answers that the real sins were those of its princes, who paid the penalty.

A hired captain, Machiavelli says, is either an excellent soldier or he is not, and in either case the prince who employs him is in danger. If the man is excellent, he cannot be trusted, because he will always aim at his own greatness, either by crushing the master who pays him or by crushing others against his master's wishes. If he is not, he will simply ruin the prince in the ordinary way, by losing.

If someone objects that every man with weapons behaves like this, Machiavelli answers that armies are commanded either by a prince or by a republic. The prince must go in person and act as captain, while the republic must send its own citizens and replace any who prove unskilful or hold the able ones within the law. Rome and Sparta stood armed and free for many centuries, he notes, and the Swiss in his own day are the most armed and the most free of all.

Ancient history, Machiavelli says, teaches the same lesson, and he gives two clear examples of it. After their first war with Rome the Carthaginians were almost crushed by their own hired soldiers, even though citizens had commanded them. After the death of Epaminondas the Thebans made Philip of Macedon captain of their army, and once the victory was won he took away their liberty.

When Duke Filippo Maria Visconti of Milan died, the Milanese hired Francesco Sforza to fight the Venetians, and he defeated the enemy at Caravaggio. Then, instead of returning his victory to his employers, he joined the beaten Venetians to oppress the Milanese, his masters. By 1450 the hired captain had made himself Duke of Milan, the same Francesco Sforza whom Machiavelli had praised earlier for rising by his own ability.

The Venetians did great things as long as they used their own gentlemen and common people at sea, but when they began to fight on land they gave up that virtue and followed the Italian custom of hiring captains. Their captain Carmagnola was brilliant yet cold in war, and since they could neither dismiss him nor trust him, they finally put him to death. Under later hired captains they met the disaster at Vailà in 1509, where, Machiavelli says, they lost in one day what had cost them eight hundred years of labour.

Florence, Machiavelli's own city, had also relied on hired captains, and she escaped harm only because their ambitions were frustrated by luck or by rivals. If the English captain Sir John Hawkwood had won, no one doubts that the Florentines would have been at his mercy, and the same was true of Paolo Vitelli, a prudent man who rose from nothing to great reputation. Had Vitelli taken Pisa, Florence would have had no remedy, for if he had gone over to the enemy she would have been lost, and if she had kept him she would have had to obey him.

Chapter thirteen turns to auxiliary arms, which are troops lent by a more powerful ruler who comes with his army to defend you, as Pope Julius II did when he asked Ferdinand of Spain for help. Such soldiers may be good in themselves, Machiavelli says, but they are always harmful to the man who calls them, for if they lose he is ruined and if they win he remains their prisoner. Julius escaped only by good luck, when the Swiss unexpectedly drove out the victorious French at Ravenna and spared him both enemies and allies.

Machiavelli recalls that the Florentines, wishing to take Pisa, brought in ten thousand French soldiers and ran more danger than at any other time of trouble. The Emperor of Constantinople, to oppose his neighbours, put ten thousand Turks into Greece, and when the war was over they refused to leave. That, he says, was how Greece began to fall under Turkish rule, and the whole disaster began with an invitation.

Whoever wishes to be unable to win, Machiavelli says dryly, should make use of such arms, for they are far more dangerous than hired ones. In them ruin is ready-made, since the soldiers are all united and all obedient to someone else, while hired men need more time and a better chance to hurt you. In short, with hired soldiers the danger is their laziness, while with borrowed ones it is their ability.

Machiavelli returns to Cesare Borgia as a model, for the duke entered the Romagna with French auxiliaries and took Imola and Forlì, then judged them unsafe and hired the Orsini and Vitelli. Finding these mercenaries doubtful, unfaithful and dangerous, he destroyed them and turned to soldiers of his own. His reputation grew at every step, Machiavelli says, and it never stood higher than when everyone saw that he was the complete master of his own arms.

Hiero of Syracuse, who had been made captain of the army by his fellow citizens, quickly saw that hired troops were of little use, because their leaders were condottieri like those of Machiavelli's own day. Seeing that he could neither keep them nor dismiss them, he had them all killed, and from then on he made war with his own arms and not with other men's. It was a ruthless remedy, but it shows how sharply Machiavelli draws the line between a ruler's own forces and the rest.

Machiavelli borrows a story from the Old Testament: when young David offered to fight the giant Goliath, King Saul tried to encourage him by lending him his own armour. As soon as David had it on his back, he refused it, saying that he could not use it well and that he preferred to meet his enemy with his own sling and knife. The lesson, Machiavelli concludes, is that the arms of others either fall from your back, or weigh you down, or hold you tight.

Charles VII of France, who freed his country from the English, built an army of his own, but his son Louis XI abolished the infantry and began to hire Swiss troops. This mistake, repeated by later kings, made French soldiers believe that they could not win without the Swiss, and Machiavelli sees in it the root of the kingdom's dangers. Without arms of its own, he concludes, no principality is secure, for it depends wholly on fortune, and nothing is so weak as the fame of a power that does not rest on its own strength.

A prince, Machiavelli says in chapter fourteen, should have no other aim or thought, and take up no other craft, than war and its discipline, for it is the one art expected of a ruler. It can keep those who are born princes in their place and often lifts private men to the rank, whereas rulers who cared more for comforts than for arms have always lost their states. Francesco Sforza became Duke of Milan because he was armed, and his sons, who fled the hardships of soldiering, fell from dukes to private men.

In peacetime the prince must train even harder than in war, Machiavelli says, and he can do so by action and by thought. For action, he should hunt often, which hardens the body and teaches him how mountains rise, valleys open, plains lie and rivers and marshes run. Such knowledge serves him twice, helping him to defend his own country and to grasp quickly any other region, since the hills and rivers of Tuscany resemble those of other provinces.

Machiavelli holds up Philopoemen, prince of the Achaeans, who in peacetime thought of nothing but the ways of war. When he walked in the country with his friends, he would often stop and ask what an army should do if the enemy held that hill and his own men stood here. He talked through every case that can befall an army, hearing his friends' opinions and giving his own with reasons, so that no accident in real war found him without a remedy.

For the training of the mind, Machiavelli says, the prince should read history and study the actions of excellent men, noting what caused their victories and defeats, so that he can imitate the first and avoid the second. Above all he should choose a hero to follow, as Alexander followed Achilles, Caesar followed Alexander and Scipio followed Cyrus, whose life Xenophon wrote. A wise prince is never idle in peaceful times but builds up a store of experience, so that when fortune changes she finds him ready to resist her.

Many writers have already described how a prince should treat his subjects and friends, Machiavelli says, and he fears that he will seem presumptuous for departing from their rules. His aim, however, is to write something useful for anyone who understands, and so he prefers to follow the effective truth of a matter rather than an imagined picture of it. Many have invented republics and principalities that have never been seen and that never existed in fact.

How men actually live, Machiavelli declares, is so far from how they ought to live that anyone who gives up what is done for what ought to be done learns his own ruin rather than his safety. A man who insists on being good in every respect is bound to come to grief among so many who are not good. A prince who wants to survive, therefore, must learn to be able not to be good, and to use or not use that ability as necessity requires.

All men, and above all princes, are known for qualities that bring them praise or blame: one is thought generous, another miserly, one cruel and another merciful, one faithless and another faithful. Everyone would agree that it would be wonderful for a prince to have all the qualities thought good, Machiavelli says, but human nature does not allow it. He must therefore be prudent enough to avoid the faults that would lose him his state, and he need not worry about the bad name that comes from vices without which he can hardly save it.

If one looks closely, Machiavelli says, something that appears to be virtue will bring a prince to ruin if he follows it, while something that appears to be vice will bring him security and well-being. The warning is aimed at rulers who are anxious to be admired and who mistake a good reputation for a safe state. It is one of the most debated sentences in the book, since readers disagree about whether it describes the world or recommends a way of behaving.

Machiavelli grants that it would be good to be held generous, but he argues that generosity used so that you are known for it does a prince harm. To keep such a name he cannot omit any kind of splendour, and so he will use up all his means in such displays and will be forced in the end to burden his people with heavy taxes. This begins to make him hated by his subjects, and as he grows poor, he is little respected by anyone.

A prince who has offended many and rewarded few feels the first trouble and falls at the first danger, and if he then draws back, he at once earns the name of miser. A prudent ruler, Machiavelli says, should not mind that name, because his thrift means that his revenues are enough and he can defend himself without burdening his people. In the end he will be thought generous towards all those from whom he does not take, who are countless, and stingy only towards the few to whom he does not give.

In his own time, Machiavelli observes, great things have been done only by those who were thought miserly, while the generous have been ruined. Pope Julius II used a name for generosity to win the papacy and then dropped it to make war, while the King of France has fought many wars without special taxes, thanks to his thrift. The King of Spain, he adds, would never have finished so many enterprises if he had been thought generous.

Someone may object that Caesar came to power through generosity, and that many others have reached high rank by being thought generous. Machiavelli replies that a man is either already a prince or on the way to becoming one: in the second case generosity is necessary, but in the first it does damage. Caesar was one who wanted to win power in Rome, and if he had survived without moderating his expenses once he held it, he would have destroyed the empire.

The prince who goes out with armies, feeds on booty, sacks and ransoms and handles the property of others needs this generosity, Machiavelli says, or his soldiers would not follow him. Of what belongs neither to him nor to his subjects he can be a lavish giver, as Cyrus, Caesar and Alexander were. Spending the wealth of others does not take away his reputation but adds to it, and only spending his own wealth does him harm.

There is nothing that consumes itself like generosity, Machiavelli says, for while you use it, you lose the ability to go on using it, and you become either poor and despised or, to escape poverty, greedy and hated. A prince must guard above all against being despised and hated, and generosity leads to both. It is therefore wiser, in his view, to accept the name of miser, which brings shame without hatred, than to be forced into the name of plunderer, which brings shame with hatred.

Every prince should wish to be thought merciful and not cruel, Machiavelli says, but he must take care not to use his mercy badly. Cesare Borgia was held to be cruel, and yet his cruelty reorganised the Romagna, united it and brought it to peace and loyalty. Seen in that light, Machiavelli argues, he was more merciful than the people of Florence, who allowed Pistoia to be destroyed rather than be called cruel.

A prince should not mind the bad name of cruelty if it keeps his subjects united and faithful, Machiavelli says, because a few harsh examples will make him kinder than those who let disorder grow out of pity. Disorder leads to murders and robberies that harm the whole community, whereas the punishments ordered by a prince fall on single persons. A new prince, he adds, cannot escape the name of cruel, since new states are full of dangers, as Virgil makes Dido say.

Even so, Machiavelli adds, the prince must be slow to believe and slow to act, and he must not let himself be frightened by shadows. He should proceed with moderation, prudence and humanity, so that too much confidence does not make him careless and too much distrust does not make him impossible to live with. The balance he recommends is hard to hold, for a ruler is always tempted to believe flatterers or to suspect everyone.

From this arises a famous question, whether it is better to be loved than feared or the other way round. The answer, Machiavelli says, is that one would wish to be both, but since the two are hard to join together, it is much safer to be feared than loved if one of them must be lacking. The claim is a judgment about safety, not about goodness, and readers have argued over it ever since.

Of men in general, Machiavelli says, one can say that they are ungrateful, fickle, deceitful, shy of danger and greedy for gain. While you do them good they are wholly yours, offering you their blood, their goods, their lives and even their children, as long as the need is far away. When it comes near, he adds, they turn away, and a prince who has relied on their words alone is ruined.

Friendships bought with money and not won by greatness of spirit, Machiavelli says, are paid for but not possessed, and when the time of need comes they cannot be spent. Men hesitate less to hurt someone who makes himself loved than someone who makes himself feared, because love is held by a chain of obligation that wicked men break whenever their own interest calls. Fear, by contrast, rests on a dread of punishment, and that dread never leaves men for a moment.

A prince must make himself feared in such a way that, if he does not win love, he at least escapes hatred. The two can go together, Machiavelli says, if the prince keeps his hands off the property and the women of his subjects and takes a life only for an obvious cause. Above all he should leave other people's property alone, because men forget the death of a father more quickly than the loss of an inheritance.

With an army under his command, Machiavelli says, a prince must not mind the name of cruel at all, since without it no army is kept united or ready for action. He points to Hannibal, who led a huge army made up of countless peoples through foreign lands, and in good and bad fortune alike never faced a quarrel among his men or a revolt against himself. That calm, in Machiavelli's judgment, came from Hannibal's inhuman cruelty joined to his endless other virtues, which made his soldiers both revere and fear him.

The opposite case, Machiavelli says, is Scipio, a man rare in all of history, whose armies rebelled in Spain because his excessive mercy gave the soldiers more licence than discipline allows. In the Senate, Fabius Maximus reproached him for corrupting the Roman army, and when a legate of Scipio's destroyed the city of Locri, Scipio neither avenged the Locrians nor punished the legate. Such softness would have darkened his fame if he had held absolute power, but as he lived under the Senate, the flaw was hidden and even turned to his glory.

Returning to his question, Machiavelli concludes that men love as they please but fear as the prince pleases, and that a wise ruler should therefore build on what is his own and not on what belongs to others. Love cannot be commanded, but fear can be arranged, and so the prince should rely on the second while taking care never to slide into hatred. Whether this advice is wise or merely cold is something readers have debated for centuries.

Everyone understands how praiseworthy it is for a prince to keep his word and to live with integrity rather than cunning, Machiavelli says. Yet experience in his own time shows that the princes who have done great things have been those who cared little for keeping faith and knew how to confuse men's minds with craft. In the end, he claims, they overcame the princes who had relied on honesty.

There are two ways of fighting, Machiavelli explains: one with laws and the other with force, the first proper to men and the second to beasts. Since the first is often not enough, a prince must know how to use both the beast and the man. The ancient writers taught this in disguise, he says, when they told how Achilles and other princes were raised by the centaur Chiron, a teacher who was half beast and half man.

Of all the beasts, Machiavelli says, a prince should pick the fox and the lion, because the lion cannot defend himself against traps and the fox cannot defend himself against wolves. He must therefore be a fox to recognise the traps and a lion to frighten the wolves. Those who rely on the lion alone, he adds, simply do not understand their business.

A prudent ruler, Machiavelli says, cannot and should not keep his word when doing so turns against him and the reasons that made him promise have disappeared. If all men were good, the advice would be bad, but since they are wicked and would not keep faith with him, he need not keep it with them. Princes, he adds, have never lacked respectable reasons for breaking their word, and the one who has known best how to play the fox has come out best.

It is necessary, Machiavelli says, to know how to disguise this fox's nature well, and to be a great pretender and dissembler. Men are so simple, and so ruled by the needs of the moment, that anyone who sets out to deceive will always find somebody willing to be deceived.
