This is among the bleakest sentences in the book, and it is one of the reasons why its author's name became a byword for cunning.

Machiavelli cannot resist a recent example in Pope Alexander VI, who never did or thought anything but deceive men, and who always found people willing to be deceived. No man, he says, was ever more effective in declaring a thing and swearing greater oaths to it while observing it less. Yet his deceptions always turned out as he wished, because he understood very well this side of the world.

A prince need not possess all the good qualities in fact, Machiavelli says, but he must certainly seem to possess them, and he even claims that having and always practising them is harmful. He should appear merciful, faithful, humane, upright and religious, and be so as long as he can, yet his mind must be ready to turn the other way when the winds of fortune require it. Especially a new prince cannot keep all the virtues, he says, because to hold his state he is often forced to act against faith, charity, humanity and religion.

A prince must take great care, Machiavelli says, that nothing ever leaves his mouth that is not full of five qualities: mercy, faith, honesty, humanity and religion. To anyone who sees and hears him, he should seem to be made entirely of them. Nothing, he adds, is more necessary to appear to have than the last of the five, and critics have long argued whether he meant this as cynicism or as plain observation.

Men in general, Machiavelli says, judge more by their eyes than by their hands, for everyone can see but few can touch, and everyone sees what you appear to be while few feel what you are. In the actions of all men, and above all of princes, there is no court of appeal, so one looks to the result. Let a prince win and keep his state, he claims, and the means will always be judged honourable, because the crowd is taken by appearances and by outcomes.

Machiavelli ends the chapter with a sly example, a certain prince of the present day whom, he says, it is not good to name. This man preaches nothing but peace and faith, and yet he is a great enemy of both, and if he had kept either one it would many times have cost him his reputation or his state. Readers have long guessed that the king he has in mind is Ferdinand of Aragon, whom he praises for his greatness in a later chapter.

The key rule of chapter nineteen, Machiavelli says, is that a prince should avoid whatever makes him hated or despised, and if he does that, he will meet no danger from his other faults. He is hated above all when he is greedy and takes the property and women of his subjects, and he is despised when he is thought changeable, frivolous, weak or indecisive. He should guard against these faults like a reef, and show greatness, courage, gravity and strength in all that he does.

A prince who gives such an impression of himself is greatly respected, Machiavelli says, and against a man so respected it is hard to conspire and hard to attack from outside. He has two things to fear, trouble at home from his subjects and danger from abroad from foreign powers, and he can defend himself against the latter with good arms and good friends. If he has good arms, he adds, he will always have good friends, and affairs at home will stay calm as long as affairs abroad are calm.

One of the strongest remedies a prince has against conspiracies, Machiavelli says, is not to be hated by the people at large, because a plotter always hopes that the prince's death will please the people. Many conspiracies have been made and few have ended well, since a conspirator cannot act alone and must confide in men he believes to be discontented, any of whom can win a sure reward by betraying him. On the plotter's side there is only fear, jealousy and the dread of punishment, while on the prince's side stand the majesty of his office, the laws, his friends and the state.

Machiavelli gives an example from Bologna, where Annibale Bentivoglio, the prince of the city, was murdered by the conspiring Canneschi family and left behind only a baby son, Giovanni. At once the people rose and killed every one of the Canneschi, so great was the goodwill that the Bentivoglio house enjoyed. Since no adult of the family remained, the Bolognese went to Florence to fetch a young Bentivoglio who was thought to be a blacksmith's son, and he governed the city until the baby grew up.

Machiavelli praises the Parlement of France as one of the finest institutions of that well-ordered kingdom. Its founder, knowing the nobles' ambition and the people's hatred of them, set up a third judge who could rein in the great and protect the weak without making the king carry the burden of either task. From this he draws a rule for all princes, that they should leave unpopular tasks to others and keep the granting of favours for themselves.

Some will object that the Roman emperors contradict his advice, since certain good ones were overthrown, and Machiavelli answers them by looking at the emperors from Marcus Aurelius to Maximinus. In other states a prince has to deal only with the ambition of the great and the insolence of the people, but the Roman emperors faced a third difficulty in the cruelty and greed of their soldiers. The people loved quiet and therefore modest rulers, while the soldiers wanted a ruler who was fierce, cruel and rapacious, and who would treat the people harshly.

Marcus Aurelius, Machiavelli says, lived and died honoured because he inherited the empire and owed it neither to soldiers nor to people, and his many virtues kept both within bounds. Pertinax, made emperor against the soldiers' will, tried to make them live honestly, and the hatred he earned, joined to contempt for his age, ruined him within months, for hatred is won by good deeds as well as bad. Alexander Severus, so just that no man was executed without trial, was despised as a man ruled by his mother, and his army killed him.

Septimius Severus, Machiavelli says, was a very fierce lion and a very astute fox. Persuading his army on the Danube that they should march on Rome to avenge Pertinax, he reached Italy before anyone understood his plan, and the frightened Senate elected him emperor. He then fought Niger in the East while deceiving Albinus with the title of Caesar, and once Niger was dead he turned on Albinus and destroyed him.

Machiavelli then passes briskly through the emperors who came to bad ends, and he finds hatred or contempt in every case. Caracalla was a brave soldier loved by his armies, but his cruelty, including the slaughter of many in Rome and Alexandria, made the world hate him, and a centurion whose brother he had killed struck him down. Commodus, who inherited the throne, ruined himself by fighting as a gladiator, and Maximinus, a shepherd by birth, was despised for his low origin and hated for his cruelty, until his own army killed him.

Princes of his own day, Machiavelli says, have less trouble with soldiers, whose armies are not tied to the government of provinces as the Roman legions were. Nearly every prince must therefore please the people more than the soldiers, with the exception of the Turk and the Sultan, whose power rests wholly on their armies. A new prince, he concludes, should take from Severus what is needed to found a state, and from Marcus what suits keeping a state already firm.

Chapter twenty asks whether disarming subjects, dividing them or building fortresses really keeps a state safe, and Machiavelli begins with arms. A new prince, he says, has never disarmed his subjects but has always armed them, for their weapons then become his own and the doubtful become loyal. To disarm them begins by offending them, since it shows that he distrusts them, and either cowardice or lack of faith breeds hatred.

In the past, Machiavelli recalls, men held to be wise said that Pistoia should be held with factions and Pisa with fortresses, and they encouraged quarrels among their subjects. He does not think this can be a rule today, since divisions never do good, and when an enemy approaches a divided city is lost, because the weaker party joins the invader. The Venetians nourished the old Guelf and Ghibelline parties in their cities, and when they were beaten at Vailà, one party at once took courage and took the cities from them.

Princes become great, Machiavelli says, by overcoming the difficulties placed in their way, which is why Fortune raises up enemies against a new prince, so that he can climb higher on the ladder they bring. Men who were his enemies at the start, if they need support to keep themselves safe, can easily be won and will serve him more faithfully than those who trusted him from the first. Those who helped him to power only because they disliked the old rule are hard to keep as friends, since he can never satisfy them.

It has been the custom of princes to build fortresses as a bridle on those who might plot against them, and Machiavelli approves of the method because it is ancient. Yet in his own times Niccolò Vitelli demolished two fortresses at Città di Castello, and Guido Ubaldo, Duke of Urbino, razed every fortress in his duchy when he returned from exile. Fortresses, then, are useful or not according to the times, and the castle that Francesco Sforza built in Milan has caused his house more trouble than any other disorder.

The best fortress there is, Machiavelli concludes, is not to be hated by the people, for if the people hate you, your fortresses will not save you, since foreigners never lack when a people takes up arms. The one prince in his time who had benefited from a fortress was the Countess of Forlì, who after her husband's murder held out in hers until help came from Milan. Later, when Cesare Borgia attacked and the hostile people joined the invader, her fortress was of little value, and it would have been safer for her to have the people's goodwill than any walls.

Nothing makes a prince so esteemed, Machiavelli says, as great enterprises and rare examples of his own conduct, and he offers Ferdinand of Aragon, the King of Spain, as a model. Ferdinand, whom he calls almost a new prince, rose from a weak king to the first king of Christendom in fame and glory, and he began with the war on Granada, the foundation of his state. The war kept the barons of Castile so occupied with thoughts of fighting that they never thought of rebellion, and he gained power over them without their noticing.

Ferdinand paid for his armies with money from the Church and the people, and the long war in Granada laid the foundation of his military power. Under the cover of religion he also turned to what Machiavelli calls a pious cruelty, persecuting and driving out Jews and converted Jews, an act that modern readers regard as a grave injustice. Under the same cloak he attacked Africa, Italy and France, and his deeds followed one another so fast that his subjects were kept in suspense and never had time to plot against him.

A prince is also esteemed, Machiavelli says, when he is a true friend or a true enemy, that is, when he declares himself openly for one side against another, which is always more useful than staying neutral. The Roman envoy said as much to the Achaeans, when King Antiochus asked them to stay out of the war: neutrality, he warned, would leave them without favour or dignity, the prize of the winner. Irresolute princes, who follow the neutral path to avoid present dangers, are in his experience most often ruined.

If the side a prince joins wins, Machiavelli explains, the winner owes him a debt, and if it loses, the prince is sheltered and shares a fortune that may rise again. He should never ally with someone more powerful to attack others unless necessity forces him, as the Venetians did when they joined France against Milan. No state can always take safe courses, since avoiding one trouble brings another, and prudence consists in recognising which troubles are least and treating the lesser evil as a good.

Machiavelli closes the chapter with the practical duties of a ruler who wishes to be esteemed. He should honour talent in every art, and encourage his citizens to carry on their trades quietly, so that nobody hesitates to improve his property for fear it will be taken, or to open a business for fear of taxes. He should reward those who enlarge his city or state, hold festivals at suitable times of the year and meet the guilds of the city now and then, always keeping the dignity of his office.

The choice of ministers, Machiavelli says, is of no small importance to a prince, for it shows his judgment, and the first guess anyone makes about a ruler's brain is made by looking at the men around him. When they are capable and faithful he can always be thought wise, but when they are not, the first error he has made is in this choice. Everyone who knew Antonio da Venafro, the minister of Pandolfo Petrucci, prince of Siena, judged Pandolfo a very worthy man for having him.

There are three kinds of brains, Machiavelli says: one understands things by itself, another can recognise what others have understood, and the third understands neither alone nor with help. The first is excellent, the second also excellent, and the third useless, so that a prince who is not of the first kind must at least belong to the second. A man of the second kind can tell good work from bad in his minister, praising the one and correcting the other, and the minister, knowing that he cannot deceive him, stays honest.

One test of a minister never fails, Machiavelli says: if he thinks more of himself than of you and seeks his own profit in everything, he will never be good and you can never trust him. The prince, for his part, should keep a good minister loyal by honouring him, enriching him and sharing honours and duties with him, so that the man sees he cannot stand without his master. Many honours then do not make him want more honours, many riches do not make him want more riches, and many duties make him fear change.

Courts, Machiavelli warns, are full of flatterers, and men are so pleased with their own affairs and so ready to deceive themselves that they defend themselves with difficulty against this plague. There is no way to guard against flattery except to let men understand that you will not be offended by the truth. The danger is that when everyone may tell you the truth, you begin to lose respect.

The prudent prince, Machiavelli says, takes a third course: he chooses wise men in his state and gives only them the freedom to tell him the truth, and only about the matters on which he asks. He must question them about everything, listen to their opinions and then decide for himself, making each of them see that the more freely he speaks the more welcome he will be. Apart from them he should listen to no one, and hold firmly to what he has decided, or he will either fall to flatterers or change his mind so often that he is little esteemed.

Machiavelli gives a modern example in Emperor Maximilian, who kept his plans secret and took no advice, but who was talked out of them by the people around him as soon as they became known. As a result what he did one day he undid the next, nobody ever knew what he wanted, and nobody could rely on his decisions. A prince should take counsel when he wants it, not when others want, he says, for a prince who is not wise himself cannot be well advised, and good counsel must spring from his own prudence.

A new prince who follows the advice above, Machiavelli says, will appear to be an old one and will be more secure in his state than if he had grown old in it. He is watched much more closely than a hereditary prince, and when his actions are seen to be virtuous they bind men more firmly than ancient blood, because men are more taken with the present than with the past. He will then have double glory, for having founded a new principality and strengthened it with good laws, good arms, good friends and good examples, as the born prince who loses his state through lack of prudence has double shame.

When Machiavelli examines the lords of Italy who lost their states in his own day, such as the King of Naples and the Duke of Milan, he finds first a common weakness in their armies. He then sees that some of them had a hostile people, and others, though their people were friendly, did not know how to secure themselves against their nobles. States with enough strength to put an army into the field, he adds, are not lost without these faults.

Machiavelli adds the case of Philip of Macedon, not the father of Alexander but the king later beaten by Titus Quintius, whose state was small beside the might of Rome and Greece when they attacked him. Philip was a soldier who knew how to keep the people content and the great secure, and so he held out against them for many years. Even when he lost some cities in the end, he was left with his kingdom.

The Italian princes who lost their states after long rule, Machiavelli says, should blame not fortune but their own idleness, for in quiet times they never expected change, and when trouble came they thought only of running away. They hoped that their peoples, angry at the conquerors' insolence, would recall them, but a defence that depends on the favour of others is base and uncertain. Only those defences are good, certain and lasting, he concludes, that depend on yourself and your own ability.

Chapter twenty-five takes up a belief held by many, that worldly things are governed by fortune and by God so completely that human prudence cannot correct them, and that it is better to leave everything to chance. This belief has grown stronger in his own times, Machiavelli says, because of the great and unforeseen changes that people have seen every day. Thinking about the matter, he admits, he has himself sometimes been inclined to agree with those who hold it.

Yet he does not want human free will to be extinguished, and so he offers a compromise. It may be true, he says, that fortune is the arbiter of half of our actions, but she leaves the other half, or very nearly, for us to govern. Everything in the chapter that follows grows out of that one careful sentence, in which luck is large but not complete.

Machiavelli compares fortune to one of those violent rivers which, when they are angry, flood the plains, tear down trees and buildings and carry earth from one place to another. Everyone flees before such a river and everyone yields to its force, unable to hinder it in any way. The picture is a famous one, and its power lies in how well it fits the helplessness that people feel in a flood.

And yet, Machiavelli says, men can make provision in quiet times with dikes and embankments, so that when the river rises it will either flow away through a canal or lose some of its wild and harmful force. Fortune behaves in just the same way, showing her power where no resistance has been prepared and turning her force to the places where she knows that no dikes or banks have been built to hold her. The lesson is practical: preparation made before the storm is what he means by virtue.

If one looks at Italy, Machiavelli says, which is the seat of these upheavals and the country that set them in motion, one sees a land without dikes and without any bank. Had it been defended by adequate virtue, as Germany, Spain and France have been, this flood would either not have caused such great changes or would not have come here at all. That, he thinks, is enough to say about the way of opposing fortune in general, before he turns to particular rulers.

Turning to particular cases, Machiavelli notes that one sees a prince flourishing today and ruined tomorrow without any change in his nature or his qualities. The first cause, he thinks, is that a prince who leans wholly on fortune falls when fortune turns. He believes also that a prince is fortunate when his way of acting matches the spirit of the times, and unfortunate when it clashes with them.

Men pursue the goals that stand before them, which are glory and riches, in different ways, Machiavelli says, one with caution and another with impetuosity, one with violence and another with craft, and each may reach the goal. Two cautious men may end differently, and a cautious man and a bold man may be equally happy, and the explanation is nothing but the quality of the times, which agree or disagree with each man's way of acting. So two men acting differently can have the same result, and two acting in the same way can end differently.

If a man governs with caution and patience, Machiavelli says, and the times suit his way, he comes out happy, but if the times change he is ruined because he does not change his way of proceeding. No man is prudent enough to adapt, both because he cannot depart from what his nature inclines him to do and because, having always prospered on one road, he cannot be persuaded to leave it. The cautious man therefore does not know how to be bold when boldness is needed, and if he could change his nature with the times, his fortune would not change.

Pope Julius II acted impetuously in everything, Machiavelli says, and found times so well suited to this way of acting that he always came to a happy end. When he marched in person on Bologna, the Venetians were displeased and the King of Spain was uneasy, yet his sudden move left both frozen and drew France after him. No other pope, with all human prudence, would have managed it, Machiavelli adds, since if he had waited until everything was arranged, he would have met a thousand excuses and a thousand fears.

Julius's short life spared him the times that would have required caution, Machiavelli notes, and in them he would have been ruined, for he would never have left the ways to which his nature inclined him. He concludes that it is better to be impetuous than cautious, since fortune, as he puts it, is a woman who yields more readily to the bold. She is therefore the friend of the young, who are less careful and command her with more audacity, and the image, which many readers today find offensive, ends the chapter with a flourish.

The last chapter, an appeal to action, begins with Machiavelli's question to himself: are the times in Italy right for a new prince who could bring honour to himself and good to his people? He decides that so many things work together for a new prince that no earlier time seems to him better suited. The whole book has been leading to this moment, and the calm, cool reasoning of the earlier chapters now gives way to a tone of passion.

As Israel had to be enslaved for Moses to show his greatness, and the Athenians scattered for Theseus, so Italy, Machiavelli says, has had to sink low for an Italian spirit to show its worth. She is more enslaved than the Hebrews, more servile than the Persians, more scattered than the Athenians, he writes, without a head, without order, beaten, plundered, torn and overrun. She has suffered every kind of ruin, and in the depth of that ruin he sees the opening for a redeemer.

Once a spark appeared in one man, whom many readers take to be Cesare Borgia, but at the height of his career fortune rejected him, and Italy now lies as if lifeless, waiting for someone to heal her wounds. She prays to God to send a redeemer from the cruelty and insolence of the foreign invaders, Machiavelli says, and she is ready to follow any banner that someone will raise. In his view she has no better hope than the illustrious house of Medici, which with its fortune and ability and with the favour of God and the Church can make itself head of the redemption.

The great founders were rare and marvellous, Machiavelli says, but they were only men, and each had a smaller opportunity than the present one. Their enterprise was neither more just nor easier than this, and he quotes Livy that war is just for those to whom it is necessary and arms are holy where there is no other hope. He sees signs of God's favour here, as in the old story of the sea that opened and the manna that fell, but God, he adds, will not do everything, lest he take away our free will.

There is no lack of talent among the Italian people, Machiavelli argues, for in duels and small fights Italians are superior in strength, skill and wit, but in armies they do not compare. The fault lies in weak leaders, since those who know are not obeyed and everyone thinks he knows, so that in twenty years every wholly Italian army has done badly, at Taro, Alexandria, Capua, Genoa, Vailà, Bologna and Mestri. A leader who found new orders would earn more honour than any other newly risen man.

The first need, Machiavelli says, is to provide arms of their own, the true foundation of every enterprise, since nobody can have more faithful or better soldiers than his own subjects. Swiss and Spanish infantry are held to be terrible, but the Spanish cannot withstand cavalry and the Swiss fear infantry as stubborn as themselves, as the Spanish showed at Ravenna by slipping under the Germans' pikes. A new kind of infantry could therefore defeat both, and such new orders, he says, give a new prince his reputation and greatness.

Machiavelli cannot say, he writes, with what love and thirst for revenge, with what loyalty and tears, a liberator would be received in all the provinces that have suffered from foreign floods. He asks what door would be closed to such a man, and he declares that to everyone the barbarian rule stinks. He ends his whole book with Petrarch's verse that valour will take up arms against fury and the fight will be short, since the ancient courage in Italian hearts is not yet dead.

The book did not win Machiavelli the place he wanted, and the Medici did not take up its call to free Italy. Lorenzo, the young man to whom it was dedicated, died in 1519 at the age of only twenty-six, so that the hoped-for patron was gone. Machiavelli went on living in the country, writing and waiting for work, and for some years he remained an outsider in the city he had served.

In the years that followed, Machiavelli wrote the Discourses on Livy, a long study of the Roman republic that shows the side of his thinking that favoured free government. He also wrote the comedy Mandragola, a sharp and funny play that is still performed, and The Art of War, a dialogue on military affairs that was printed in 1521. Those who think of him only as the author of The Prince often forget that he was also a playwright, a historian and a defender of republics.

The Medici slowly came to trust him, and in 1520 Cardinal Giulio de' Medici asked him to write the history of Florence. When Giulio became Pope Clement VII, Machiavelli presented the finished Florentine Histories to him in Rome in 1526, and he was also asked to advise on the defence of Florence. It was the closest he came to the public life he had lost, though he never regained his old position of power.

In May 1527 Rome was sacked by imperial troops, the Medici were driven out of Florence and the republic was restored, and Machiavelli hoped to be given back his old post. The new rulers, who saw him as a servant of the Medici, passed him over, and on 21 June 1527 he died at the age of fifty-eight. He lies in the church of Santa Croce in Florence, where a monument added in 1787 carries the words, in Latin, that no praise is equal to so great a name.

The Prince was never printed in Machiavelli's lifetime, and for years it passed from reader to reader in handwritten copies, so that his friends and a few powerful men knew it long before the public did. In 1532, five years after his death, it was printed in both Rome and Florence, with the permission of Pope Clement VII, the same Giulio de' Medici who had once commissioned his history. From that moment it spread across Europe, and with it the argument about its meaning began.

Soon the book had many enemies as well as many readers, and some of its critics were fierce. Reginald Pole, an English cardinal, wrote that it seemed to him to have been written by the finger of Satan, and in 1559 the Catholic Church placed all of Machiavelli's works on its Index of forbidden books. The ban could not stop people from reading it, and in many countries it only made the book more famous.

In Elizabethan England the name of Machiavelli became a theatrical shorthand for scheming, and playgoers met a stock figure of the plotting Machiavel who smiled while he planned murder. Christopher Marlowe let a character called Machiavel speak the prologue of his play The Jew of Malta, and Shakespeare, in a play about Henry VI, wrote of the murderous Machiavel. From such stage villains the word Machiavellian came to mean cunning, deceitful and ruthless, a meaning that has little to do with the careful man who wrote the book.

Frederick of Prussia wrote an Anti-Machiavel while still crown prince, and it was published in 1740, edited by Voltaire, soon after he became king. It argued that rulers should be honest, just and the servants of their people, yet within months he sent his army into Silesia, a province of Austria, without declaring war. Critics have long enjoyed the irony, though some add that a young king in a dangerous age may have found his own book hard to follow.

Not everyone judged the book harshly, and some of its most striking defenders were writers who disliked kings. The French thinker Rousseau wrote in 1762 that Machiavelli pretended to give lessons to kings but in fact gave great lessons to peoples, so that The Prince was really the book of republicans. In the nineteenth century Italian patriots took his last chapter as a call for national unity, and when Italy became a single kingdom in 1861 they felt that his appeal had at last been answered.

Two Italian words carry much of the book's meaning: virtù, which means skill, energy and courage in action and not simple goodness, and fortuna, which means luck and the pressure of circumstances. The saying that the end justifies the means, often credited to Machiavelli, does not appear in The Prince in those words. What he does write, in chapter eighteen, is that in the actions of princes, where there is no court of appeal, one looks to the end, and readers still argue about how far he approved of this.

Five hundred years later, scholars still disagree about what kind of book The Prince really is. Some read it as plain and honest advice from a man who had seen power at work, while others take it as a warning to ordinary people, a bitter satire on princes or a clever application for a job. The different readings are possible because Machiavelli was both the cold analyst of the prince and the passionate friend of republics, and the two voices never quite agree.

Business leaders and managers still find ideas worth using in The Prince: see trouble early, choose honest advisers, resist flatterers, build strength of your own and remember that people judge by what they see. Yet it was written for a ruler of 1513, who held power over life and death, and its advice about cruelty and deceit belongs to that world and not to a modern workplace. A reader gets most from the book by separating its sharp observations about human nature from its harsher recommendations.

Machiavelli began as a clerk who lost everything and ended as the author of a short book that has outlived kings, popes and empires. It teaches foresight, shows how power really works and leaves open the hardest question of all, which is how far a good purpose can excuse hard means. The best way to read it is closely and critically, setting it beside other views, and then reaching a conclusion of your own.
